subject: rla
title: Main Idea, Supporting Details, and Summarizing
objectives: You will tell the topic of a text from its main idea and state a main idea as a complete sentence.
You will find stated and implied main ideas in paragraphs and whole passages.
You will identify the supporting details that develop a main idea and choose the detail that best supports a claim.
You will write and choose accurate, objective summaries of informational texts.
You will recognize the four common answer traps: too narrow, too broad, not stated, and distorted.

slides.title: Main Idea, Supporting Details, and Summarizing
slides.board:
Week 1 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Tell a topic from a main idea
  • Find stated and implied main ideas
  • Pick the details that prove a point
  • Write and choose strong summaries
  • Spot the four answer traps

Plan: Warm-up · Learn and practice together · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: Welcome to week 1 of Reasoning Through Language Arts. This skill sits underneath almost every reading question on the GED: what is this text mostly about, and how do I know? It drives many Social Studies and Science questions too, and the extended response depends on it. By the end of the hour you should be able to say what any paragraph is mostly about, prove it with details, and boil a whole passage down to a few sentences.
ask: When you read an article online, how do you decide if it was worth your time? (expected: any honest answer; listen for “I figure out what it's mostly about” and build on it)

slides.title: Readiness check
slides.board:
Answer out loud.

  1. Which is a complete sentence? (a) Bus routes in Riverside (b) The city cut the Riverside bus route.
  2. What does the word however signal?
  3. Say this in your own words: “The proposal was met with widespread opposition.”
  4. Which word does not belong: apples, pears, carrots, plums? What do the others share?
steps: 1. (b) is a sentence: it has a subject and a verb and makes a claim. (a) is only a phrase.
2. However signals a contrast or turn: what comes next pushes back against what came before.
3. Sample: “Many people were against the plan.”
4. Carrots do not belong; the others are fruits. Finding what details share is exactly how you will find a main idea.

notes.say: This is week 1, so the warm-up checks readiness, not last week's work. Each question previews a move we will use today: telling a phrase from a sentence (topic vs. main idea), noticing a turn word, putting an idea in your own words (summarizing), and finding what items have in common (the umbrella test). Give the student about a minute for each, and do not rescue too fast.
notes.answer: 1. (b). 2. A contrast or a turn in the writer's thinking. 3. Any accurate restatement, such as “Lots of people opposed the plan.” 4. Carrots; apples, pears, and plums are fruits.
notes.watch: If the student struggles with question 3 (paraphrase), note it: summarizing will need extra support. Offer the frame “In other words, …” and keep going.

slides.title: Headline it
slides.board:
When the Riverside bus route was cut last spring, many former riders bought used cars, carpooled, or stopped making some trips. One in five said they had turned down a job or a class because they could not get there. The transit agency now plans to restore part of the route.

Write a headline of 8 words or fewer.
steps: Weak: “Riverside bus route.” This names only the topic.
Weak: “One in five turned down jobs.” This names only one detail.
Strong: “Bus cut left riders stranded; agency backtracks.” This covers the whole paragraph.

notes.say: Give the student one minute to write a headline. A headline is a main idea in disguise: it has to tell a reader what the whole paragraph is about in very few words. When they share theirs, compare it with the two weak headlines first, then the strong one, and ask which one a busy reader would need.
ask: Does your headline cover the cut, the effect on riders, and the agency's plan? (expected: at least the cut and its effect)
notes.answer: Accept any headline of 8 words or fewer that says the cut hurt riders, with or without the agency's plan. Examples: “Bus route cut left many riders stranded”; “Riverside cut hurt riders; agency restores part.”
notes.watch: A headline that is only a phrase (“Riverside bus cuts”) is a topic. Ask, “What happened because of the cut?”

slides.title: Topic vs. main idea
slides.board:
What it isExample
TopicThe subject, a word or phrasecity parks
Main ideaThe author's point about the topic, a complete sentenceCity parks improve residents' health and bring neighbors together.

Test: A main idea can be true or false. A topic cannot.

Paragraph → main idea · Whole passage → central idea

notes.say: The topic is what a text is about; the main idea is what the author says about it. Write both on the board and ask which one you could argue with. Only the sentence makes a claim, so only the sentence can be true or false. That gives the student a test they can run on their own answers forever. Point out that the GED says “central idea” for a whole passage; it works the same way.
ask: Is “the high cost of child care” a topic or a main idea? (expected: topic; it is a phrase and cannot be true or false)
Turn it into a main idea. (expected: any claim, such as “The high cost of child care keeps some parents from working.”)
notes.watch: Students often think a long, specific phrase is a main idea. Length does not matter; ask, “Is it a sentence that makes a claim?”

slides.title: Find the topic, then the main idea
slides.board:
“Public libraries have quietly become some of the busiest job centers in many communities. On a typical weekday, visitors use library computers to search job listings and submit applications. Librarians help patrons format résumés. Many libraries also host free workshops on interviewing.”

What is the topic? State the main idea as a sentence.
steps: Step 1, topic: public libraries.
Step 2, the author's point: sentence 1 says they have become busy job centers.
Step 3, check the details: computers for applications, résumé help, interview workshops. All are job help.
Main idea: “Public libraries now play a major role in helping people find work.” It can be true or false, so it passes the test.

notes.say: Model the thinking out loud, one step at a time. Name the topic first, then ask what the author says about it, then check the details. The check is what makes this reliable: if every detail fits, the main idea is right.
ask: Would “Librarians help people with résumés” work as the main idea? (expected: no; it is one detail)

slides.title: Where main ideas live
slides.board:
1. First sentence: most common, not guaranteed
  2. After a hook or turn: a story, a question, or a belief, then however, but, in fact
  3. Last sentence: details first, point last
  4. Nowhere: implied; you write it

Whole passage: title · end of paragraph 1 · last paragraph

Check: do the other sentences explain or prove it?

notes.say: The first sentence is the most common spot, and that is exactly why it is a trap: test writers know students grab it. Teach the four locations and the one check that works in every case: if the other sentences explain or prove a sentence, that sentence is the main idea. For a full passage, the title, the end of the first paragraph, and the conclusion are the places to look.
ask: Why would a writer start with a belief they disagree with? (expected: to set up their own point by contrast; it grabs attention)
notes.watch: Some students learn “first sentence” as a rule. Keep repeating: it is a likely spot, not a rule. Always check.

slides.title: When the first sentence is a trap
slides.board:
(1) Many people believe getting in shape requires a gym or expensive equipment. (2) A brisk 30-minute walk, however, strengthens the heart and lungs. (3) Walking is easier on the knees than running. (4) It requires only comfortable shoes. (5) For many adults, walking may be the simplest way to build a regular exercise habit.

Which sentence states the main idea?
steps: Sentence 1 is a belief. However in sentence 2 shows the author disagrees.
Sentences 2–4 give three reasons: heart and lungs, easy on knees, needs only comfortable shoes.
Sentence 5 pulls the reasons together.
Main idea: sentence 5. Umbrella check: all three reasons fit under “simplest way.”

notes.say: Most students will pick sentence 1. Let them, then show why it fails: the word “however” tells us the author disagrees with it. Walk through the three reasons and show that sentence 5 pulls them together. This is the details-first, point-last pattern.
ask: What word warned us about sentence 1? (expected: however)

slides.title: Find it together
slides.board:
(1) Most people think of bees only as honey makers. (2) Their bigger job, though, is pollination. (3) As bees move from flower to flower, they carry pollen that many fruit and vegetable plants need to produce food. (4) Without bees, farmers would harvest far fewer apples, almonds, and blueberries.

Topic? Which sentence is the main idea?
steps: Topic: bees.
Sentence 1 is a common belief; though in sentence 2 signals the turn.
Sentences 3 and 4 explain why pollination matters.
Main idea: sentence 2, “Their bigger job, though, is pollination.”

notes.say: Now the student leads and you guide. Ask for the topic first, then ask them to find a turn word. Reveal each step only after the student answers it.
ask: What is the turn word? (expected: though)
Do sentences 3 and 4 prove sentence 2? (expected: yes; they show why pollination is the bigger job)
notes.answer: Topic: bees. Main idea: sentence 2. Sentence 1 is the belief the author moves past; sentences 3–4 support sentence 2.
notes.watch: If the student picks sentence 4, ask, “Is that about all of what bees do, or one result?” It is one result of pollination, so it is a detail.

slides.title: Supporting details and the umbrella test
slides.board:
Supporting details explain or prove the main idea: facts, numbers, examples, reasons, quotations.

Umbrella test: the main idea must cover every important detail.

  • Covers one detail → too narrow
  • Covers far more than the text → too broad
  • Fits under no umbrella → not relevant

notes.say: Draw an umbrella on the shared screen if you can. The main idea is the umbrella; every detail must fit under it. If a statement covers only one detail, the umbrella is too small. If it covers the whole world, it is too big. This picture becomes the student's main tool for eliminating answer choices.
ask: For the bee paragraph, is “Bees carry pollen” too narrow, too broad, or just right? (expected: too narrow)
What about “Insects are important to the planet”? (expected: too broad)
notes.watch: A too-narrow choice is usually true, which is why students pick it. Teach them that true is not enough.

slides.title: Which detail best supports the claim?
slides.board:
Claim: “A credit score can affect much more than whether you get a loan.”

A. Credit scores range from 300 to 850.
B. Landlords often check credit before renting an apartment.
C. Many people never check their own score.
D. Banks use credit scores to approve loans.
steps: Restate: credit matters for things other than loans.
A: a fact about scores; it shows nothing they affect. Out.
C: about people's habits, not what scores affect. Out.
D: about loans, the one thing the claim says to look beyond. Out.
B: credit affects housing. It proves the claim.

notes.say: Model the “best supports” method: restate the claim, then ask of each choice, “If this is true, does it prove the claim?” Several choices are true. Only one proves this specific claim. Eliminate out loud so the student hears the reason for each.
ask: Which wrong choice was most tempting, and why? (expected: usually D, because it is true and about credit)

slides.title: Which sentence does not belong?
slides.board: (1) The new community center has made life easier for families on the east side. (2) Its free after-school program runs until 6 p.m., so parents can finish their shifts. (3) A clinic on the first floor offers checkups without a long drive. (4) The building's architect also designed the county courthouse. (5) On weekends, the gym is open for youth basketball.
steps: Main idea: sentence 1, the center makes life easier for east-side families.
Sentences 2, 3, and 5 each show something that makes life easier.
Sentence 4 is about the architect. It does not show life getting easier. Remove it.

notes.say: This is the GED editing version of the umbrella test: which sentence should be removed? Have the student state the main idea first, then test each sentence against it. The off-topic sentence is about the same building, which is what makes it tricky.
ask: What is the main idea? (expected: sentence 1)
Which sentence would you cut, and why? (expected: 4; it is about the building's designer, not about helping families)
notes.answer: Remove sentence 4. Sentences 2, 3, and 5 support the main idea in sentence 1.

slides.title: Implied main ideas
slides.board:
No sentence states the point? Build it yourself.

  1. List the details in a few words.
  2. What do they have in common?
  3. What does the author want me to understand?
  4. Write one complete sentence.
  5. Test it with the umbrella.

Frame: “These details all show that ______.”

notes.say: Some writers never state the point; they trust the reader to see it. Teach the five steps as a routine, not a guess. The frame “These details all show that…” gets most adult learners unstuck. Remind them that the result must still pass the true-or-false test and the umbrella test.
ask: Why might a writer leave the main idea unstated? (expected: to let facts speak for themselves; to make the reader think; common in stories and news reports)

slides.title: Building an implied main idea
slides.board:
In 2015, Bellport had four grocery stores. Today it has one, on the far edge of town. Residents without cars take two buses to reach it. Meanwhile, the number of convenience stores selling mostly packaged snacks has doubled. Fewer than half of Bellport families eat fresh vegetables on most days.

What is the implied main idea?
steps: List: fewer grocery stores · last one far away · long bus trips · more snack shops · fewer families eat vegetables.
In common: healthy food has become hard to get.
Write: “The loss of grocery stores has made it hard for many Bellport residents to get fresh, healthy food.”
Test: every detail fits. “Bellport has more snack shops” is too narrow; “Americans do not eat enough vegetables” is too broad.

notes.say: Work the five steps visibly. Write the list of details in short phrases so the student sees how small the notes can be. Then show one too-narrow and one too-broad version so the umbrella test becomes concrete.

slides.title: Implied main idea: your lead
slides.board:
Last year, the clinic's phone line answered only about half of its calls. Patients waited an average of 40 minutes on hold. Many gave up and went to the emergency room instead, which cost them and the hospital far more.

State the implied main idea in one sentence.
steps: List: half of calls unanswered · 40-minute waits · patients went to the ER · ER cost more.
In common: the phone problems pushed patients toward costly care.
Sample: “The clinic's overloaded phone line kept patients from getting care and sent them to the more expensive emergency room.”

notes.say: The student runs the five steps while you prompt. Ask for the list first; do not accept a main idea until the list is done. When they give a sentence, have them run the umbrella test out loud.
ask: What do the details have in common? (expected: the phone line failed, and that led to costly ER visits)
notes.answer: Any sentence that connects the phone problems to the costly emergency room visits is correct, for example: “The clinic's overloaded phone line pushed patients into the more expensive emergency room.”
notes.watch: A common answer is “Patients waited 40 minutes on hold.” That is one detail. Ask, “And what happened because of it?”

slides.title: Writing a summary
slides.board:
1. State the central idea in one sentence.
  2. Add 2–4 key points, about one per major part.
  3. Drop small examples, exact numbers, quotations.
  4. Add nothing: no opinions, no outside facts.
  5. Check every sentence against the text.

Short · objective · your own words · accurate

notes.say: A summary is a short, objective restatement of the central idea and key points. Stress the two biggest mistakes: retelling everything, and adding an opinion. One good habit: cover the text, write from memory, then uncover and check. That keeps students from copying and shows what they really understood.
ask: Is a good summary about as long as the original? (expected: no; much shorter)
Name two things that do not belong in a summary. (expected: any two of opinions, minor details or examples, outside facts, copied sentences)

slides.title: Summarizing a short passage
slides.board:
[1] Many small towns rely on volunteer firefighters. [2] Over the past twenty years, these departments have struggled to find volunteers. Training takes more hours than it once did, and more people work far from home. [3] To attract members, some departments now offer small payments for each call, help with college costs, or free training for a paid career.

Write a two-sentence summary.
steps: Central idea: volunteer departments are short of members and are trying new ways to recruit.
Key points: [1] towns rely on volunteers · [2] harder to find them: longer training, long commutes · [3] payments, college help, training.

Summary: “Many small towns depend on volunteer firefighters, but departments struggle to find members because training takes longer and many people work far from home. To recruit, some now offer small payments, college help, or career training.”
Weak: “Firefighters are heroes, and everyone should volunteer.” Opinion, and no key points.

notes.say: Show the student how a summary follows the passage's structure: one key point per part. Then contrast it with a weak summary so they can see exactly what goes wrong.

slides.title: Summary: keep or cut?
slides.board:
An article explains that apprentices earn a paycheck while learning a skilled trade, that they finish with a credential and experience, and that employers get workers who are trained in the exact skills they need and who stay longer.

Keep or cut for a summary?

  1. Apprentices earn pay while learning a trade.
  2. Welding is one trade the article mentions.
  3. Employers benefit because apprentices stay longer.
  4. Apprenticeships are better than college.
  5. Workers finish with a credential and experience.
steps: 1. Keep: the central idea.
2. Cut: a minor example.
3. Keep: a key point (employers' benefit).
4. Cut: an opinion the article never states.
5. Keep: a key point (workers' benefit).

notes.say: The student decides keep or cut and gives a reason for each. The reason matters more than the answer: “minor example” and “opinion” are the two reasons to cut.
ask: Why cut number 4 if some people believe it? (expected: the article never says it; a summary adds nothing)

slides.title: The four answer traps
slides.board:
TrapLooks likeAsk
Too narrowA true detailDoes it cover everything?
Too broadBigger than the textDoes the text discuss all this?
Not statedOpinion or outside factWhere does it say that?
DistortedA detail changed or exaggeratedDoes it match exactly?

notes.say: GED wrong answers are written to sound reasonable, and almost all of them fall into these four traps. From now on, every time you eliminate a choice together, name the trap out loud. When the student misses a question in Practice, the first question to ask is “Which trap got you?”
ask: Which trap do you think fools people most often? (expected: usually too narrow or distorted, because those choices use the passage's own words)

slides.title: Name the trap
slides.board:
Ten years ago, Main Street in Corbin had six empty storefronts. Since then, several people who work from home moved to Corbin for its lower rents. Today Main Street has a coffee shop, a shared office, and a bike shop, and only one storefront is empty.

Label each: (a) Remote workers have helped revive Corbin's Main Street. (b) Corbin has a new coffee shop. (c) Working from home is better than working in an office. (d) Remote workers have filled every empty storefront in Corbin.
steps: (a) Just right: covers the empty stores, the newcomers, and the new businesses.
(b) Too narrow: one business out of three.
(c) Not stated: an opinion the paragraph never gives.
(d) Distorted: one storefront is still empty.

notes.say: Read the paragraph, then take the statements one at a time. Name the trap and give the evidence for each. Point out that (b) and (d) both use words from the paragraph; that is what makes those traps dangerous.

slides.title: Your turn: topic, main idea, umbrella
slides.board:
1. Topic or main idea? (a) “The rising cost of rent” (b) “Rising rents are pushing young workers out of the city.”

2. (1) Many people fear sharks. (2) Yet sharks kill only a handful of people worldwide in a typical year. (3) People, meanwhile, kill millions of sharks every year. (4) The real danger runs the other way. Which sentence is the main idea?

3. Label for the shark paragraph: “Sharks kill few people” · “Ocean animals face many dangers.”
steps: 1. (a) topic; (b) main idea.
2. Sentence 4. Sentences 2 and 3 prove it; sentence 1 is the belief it answers.
3. “Sharks kill few people”: too narrow. “Ocean animals face many dangers”: too broad.

notes.say: Start a three-minute timer and stay quiet while the student works. When time is up, have them give each answer with a reason before you reveal anything.
notes.answer: 1. (a) is a topic (a phrase); (b) is a main idea (a sentence that can be true or false). 2. Sentence 4: humans are the bigger danger to sharks; sentences 2 and 3 are the evidence, and “Yet” turns away from sentence 1. 3. Too narrow (one detail); too broad (the paragraph is only about sharks and people).
notes.watch: On problem 2, students who pick sentence 1 are still choosing the first sentence by habit. Ask them to find the turn word (“Yet”).

slides.title: Your turn: implied main idea and support
slides.board:
Maria's Diner used to close at 3 p.m. Last year it began staying open until 9. It hired four new cooks, added a dinner menu, and now hosts a trivia night on Thursdays. Its parking lot, once empty after lunch, is full most evenings.

1. State the implied main idea.

2. Which detail best shows the evening business is succeeding: closing time, the dinner menu, or the parking lot?

3. Is “The diner hosts trivia night” a good main idea?
steps: 1. Sample: “Maria's Diner has grown into a busy evening spot.”
2. The parking lot. Only it shows customers actually coming.
3. No: too narrow, one detail.

notes.say: Three minutes. The student works alone; you watch the clock. Then ask for each answer with a reason.
notes.answer: 1. Any sentence saying the diner's evening business has grown and is busy. 2. The full parking lot; the old closing time shows where it started, and the dinner menu shows what the diner did, not whether customers came. 3. No; it is too narrow.
notes.watch: On problem 2, “added a dinner menu” is tempting. Ask, “Does adding a menu prove anyone came to eat?”

slides.title: Your turn: summaries
slides.board:
1. Write a one-sentence summary of the bee paragraph from earlier.

2. What is wrong with this summary of the firefighter passage: “Firefighters are heroes, and everyone should volunteer”?

3. In a summary of the Bellport passage, would you include “Residents without cars take two buses”? Why or why not?
steps: 1. Sample: “Bees matter most because they pollinate many of the plants that produce our food.”
2. It adds an opinion and leaves out every key point.
3. Cut it: a minor detail. “The last store is far away” covers it.

notes.say: Three to four minutes. Have the student write problem 1 rather than say it; writing forces precision. Then go through all three answers.
notes.answer: 1. Any accurate one-sentence summary that names pollination and its importance to food. 2. It is an opinion, not a summary; it includes none of the key points (shortage of volunteers, why, and how departments recruit). 3. Leave it out or fold it into “the last store is hard to reach”; the exact bus detail is minor.

slides.title: GED question: central idea
slides.board:
Community health workers are trusted local residents trained to help neighbors with their health. They visit homes, explain doctors' instructions, and help people sign up for insurance. In one county, patients who worked with them visited the emergency room less often.

Which statement best expresses the main idea?

A. Community health workers visit patients' homes.
B. Health care in America costs too much.
C. Community health workers help neighbors manage their health and use care more wisely.
D. Community health workers have replaced doctors in one county, so patients there no longer need the emergency room.
steps: A is too narrow: home visits are one of three things they do.
B is not stated: the paragraph never discusses costs nationwide.
D is distorted: they explain doctors' instructions; they do not replace doctors, and ER visits went down, not away.
C is correct: it covers what they do and the result (fewer ER visits).

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. Have the student predict the answer in their own words first, then read the choices. Then eliminate together, naming the trap each time.
ask: Before you look at the choices, what is the main idea in your words? (expected: health workers help neighbors handle their health, and it works)
notes.answer: C. A is too narrow, B is not stated (and too broad), D is distorted.

slides.title: GED question: best support
slides.board:
A passage claims that a company's switch to a four-day workweek helped it keep its workers.

Which detail best supports this claim?

A. Staff turnover fell from 20 percent to 8 percent the year after the switch.
B. Some employees used their Fridays for medical appointments.
C. The company's founder first read about the idea in a magazine.
D. Several other companies are considering the same change.
steps: B shows how workers used the day off, not whether they stayed.
C is background about where the idea came from.
D is about other companies, not this company's workers.
A is correct: fewer workers leaving is exactly what “keeping workers” means.

notes.say: Use the best-supports method: restate the claim, then test each choice with “If this is true, does it prove the claim?” Make the student say what “keep its workers” would look like in numbers.
ask: What kind of evidence would prove a company kept its workers? (expected: fewer people quitting; turnover going down)
notes.answer: A. Turnover falling from 20 percent to 8 percent directly shows more workers stayed.
notes.watch: B is tempting because it shows a real benefit to workers. A benefit is not proof that they stayed.

slides.title: GED question: best summary
slides.board:
Use the firefighter passage from earlier.

Which is the best summary?

A. Volunteer departments are short of members because training takes longer and people work far away, so some now offer pay, college help, or career training.
B. Required training now takes more hours than it once did, and more volunteers work far from home.
C. Small towns should pay all firefighters a full salary.
D. Volunteer departments have stopped training new members to save time, so they can now fill their ranks quickly.
steps: B fails coverage: it gives only the causes from paragraph 2 and leaves out the towns' reliance on volunteers and the new recruiting efforts (too narrow).
C fails objectivity: an opinion the passage never gives (not stated).
D fails accuracy: training got longer; nobody stopped training (distorted).
A is correct: the problem, its causes, and the response, accurately and without opinion.

notes.say: Run the three summary tests on each choice: coverage, accuracy, objectivity. Have the student say which test each wrong choice fails.
notes.answer: A. B is too narrow, C is not stated, D is distorted.

slides.title: GED strategy: Predict, match, test
slides.board:
1. Read the question first, then the paragraph it names.
  2. Predict: say the answer in your own words before reading the choices.
  3. Match: find the choice closest to your prediction.
  4. Test: umbrella test, and “Where does it say that?”
  5. Name the trap on each choice you cut.

Go to the paragraph the question names. Do not reread the whole passage for every question.

notes.say: Wrong answers are written to sound reasonable. If the student reads the choices before they have their own answer, the choices start doing the thinking. Predicting first keeps them in control, and it is faster. On the real test the clock matters, so going straight to the paragraph a question names saves real time.
ask: Why predict before reading the choices? (expected: so the wrong answers do not pull you off track)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• Topic = phrase. Main idea = sentence that can be true or false.
  • Check first sentences, turns (however), last sentences, or build an implied idea.
  • Best support proves the exact claim.
  • Summary: central idea + key points, no opinions.
  • Traps: too narrow, too broad, not stated, distorted.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A (Set B if under 80%) → Exit Check

notes.say: Have the student say the four traps from memory before you reveal the recap. Then walk through what comes next: the Student Lesson reviews today step by step with checks, Practice Set A has 15 GED-style questions with the reasoning behind every wrong answer, and the Exit Check confirms they are ready for week 2.
ask: What is one thing you will do differently the next time you answer a main idea question? (expected: any specific habit, such as predicting first or checking for a turn word)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Almost every reading question on the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test comes back to one question: What is this text mostly about, and how do I know? The same question shows up on the Social Studies and Science tests and in the extended response. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • tell the topic of a text from its main idea
  • find main ideas that are stated and main ideas that are implied
  • pick the supporting details that prove a point
  • write and choose strong summaries
  • spot the four answer traps that make wrong choices sound right

Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check question. You must answer it before you move on, and if you miss it, you will see exactly why that answer is wrong. Then you will move on to Practice and the Exit Check.

screens.title: Topic vs. main idea
screens.html:
The topic is the subject of a text, usually a word or short phrase. The main idea is the point the author makes about the topic, and it is always a complete sentence.

TermWhat it isExample
TopicThe subject, in a word or phraseCity parks
Main ideaThe author's point about the topic, as a sentenceCity parks improve residents' health and bring neighbors together.
Supporting detailA fact, example, number, reason, or quotation that proves the main ideaPeople who live near a park walk more each week than people who do not.

On the GED you will see main idea for a paragraph and central idea for a whole passage. They work the same way.

check.prompt: Which of these is a main idea rather than a topic?
check.hint: A main idea is a complete sentence that could be true or false.
check.explain: Only “Rising child care costs are keeping some parents out of the workforce” is a complete sentence that makes a claim. You could argue with it or prove it, so it is a main idea. The other three are phrases that name a subject. “The rising cost of child care for working families…” is the most tempting because it is long and specific, but length does not turn a topic into a main idea.
options: The rising cost of child care for working families in large cities and small towns
Rising child care costs are keeping some parents out of the workforce.
Child care in small towns
Why child care costs so much
why: This is a phrase. It names a subject but makes no claim, so it is a topic, even though it is long and specific.
This is a phrase that names a subject. Nothing about it can be true or false, so it is a topic.
This is a question-style phrase, not a statement. It names what a text might discuss but makes no point, so it is a topic.

screens.title: The true-or-false test
screens.html:
Here is a quick test you can use on any answer you write: Can it be true or false? If it can, it is a main idea. If it cannot, it is only a topic.

To turn a topic into a main idea, add what the author says about it:

Topic + the author's point = main idea

school lunches + have become healthier since new rules took effect = “School lunches have become healthier since new rules took effect.”

When you finish reading a paragraph, try to say its main idea in one sentence of your own. If all you can say is a phrase (“it's about school lunches”), go back and ask, “What is the author telling me about school lunches?”

check.prompt:
Read this: “Free school breakfast programs”

Is this a topic or a main idea? Type topic or main idea.
check.hint: Ask: could this be true or false?
check.explain: “Free school breakfast programs” is a phrase. It names a subject but makes no claim, so it fails the true-or-false test. It is a topic. To make it a main idea, add the author's point: “Free school breakfast programs help students focus in class.”

mistakes.why: It names a subject, but it does not say anything about that subject, so it cannot be true or false. A main idea would be a sentence such as “Free school breakfast programs help students focus in class.”

screens.title: Where main ideas live
screens.html:
The sentence that states a paragraph's main idea is called the topic sentence. It can show up in four places:

  1. The first sentence. This is the most common spot, but do not assume it.
  2. After a hook or transition. Some paragraphs open with a story, a question, or a common belief, and the main idea comes right after.
  3. The last sentence. Some writers give the details first and then state the point.
  4. Nowhere. The main idea is implied, and you put it into your own words.

For a whole passage, look at the title, the end of the first paragraph, and the last paragraph.

Test any sentence you think is the main idea: do the other sentences explain or prove it? If they do, you found it.

check.prompt: Read the paragraph. Click the sentence that states its main idea.
check.hint: Which sentence do the last three sentences explain or prove?
check.explain: The first sentence is a hook: it gets your attention. The second sentence makes the point: these items should be recycled, not thrown away, because recycling is safe and free. The last three sentences each name a place that recycles them, so they all prove sentence 2. That is how you know sentence 2 is the main idea.
spans: Almost every home has a drawer full of old phone chargers, dead batteries, and broken gadgets.
Throwing these items in the trash is a mistake, because many of them can be recycled safely and for free.
Many electronics stores accept old chargers and cell phones at the front counter.
Some cities hold free collection days for computers and televisions.
Many hardware stores take back used rechargeable batteries.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the first sentence. It is a hook that pictures a familiar drawer; it does not make the point. The last three sentences are examples of places that recycle these items, so each one is too narrow.

screens.title: Hooks and turns: when the first sentence is a trap
screens.html:
Writers often open with a belief they are about to challenge. Watch for signal words that mark a turn: however, but, yet, in fact, actually, though, instead. When you see one near the start of a paragraph, the main idea usually follows it.

If you pick the first sentence automatically, you may pick the exact opposite of the author's point.

example.prompt:
“Many people think of bats as frightening pests. In fact, bats are some of the most useful animals a farmer can have. Bats eat huge numbers of insects that damage crops. Some bats also pollinate plants, such as the agave. Farmers who protect bats often need less pesticide.”

Which sentence states the main idea?
steps: Sentence 1 is a common belief. “In fact” in sentence 2 signals that the author is about to disagree.
Sentence 2 makes the author's point: bats are useful to farmers.
Check: eating crop pests, pollinating plants, and reducing pesticide are all ways bats help farmers. Every detail fits.
example.answer: Main idea: “In fact, bats are some of the most useful animals a farmer can have.”

check.prompt:
“Many shoppers assume that store-brand groceries are lower in quality than name brands. However, store brands are sometimes made in the same factories as name brands. In blind taste tests, shoppers often cannot tell them apart. And store brands usually cost less.”

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the paragraph?
check.hint: Look for a signal word that shows the author disagreeing with the first sentence.
check.explain: Sentence 1 states a belief. “However” signals the turn. The remaining sentences give three reasons store brands are a good choice: same factories, same taste, lower price. The “as good as name brands and usually cost less” choice covers all three. The “Many shoppers assume” choice is the most tempting because it is a sentence from the paragraph, but it is the view the author argues against.
options: Store-brand groceries are often as good as name brands and usually cost less.
Many shoppers assume that store brands are lower in quality than name brands.
Store brands usually cost less.
Name-brand companies should stop overcharging shoppers.
why: This is the belief in the first sentence, and “However” shows the author disagrees with it. You picked the first sentence without checking for a turn.
This is true, but it is too narrow. It leaves out the factories and the taste tests.
This is not stated. The author never accuses name brands of overcharging; it is an opinion a reader might add.

screens.title: The central idea of a whole passage
screens.html:
A passage has a central idea, and each paragraph has its own main idea that helps build it. To find the central idea:

  1. Read the title.
  2. Read the end of the first paragraph, where many writers state their claim.
  3. Read the last paragraph, where many writers restate it.
  4. Jot the main idea of each body paragraph in a few words.
  5. Find the one statement that covers every paragraph.

A statement that describes only one paragraph is a main idea of that paragraph, not the central idea of the passage.

check.prompt:
School Gardens

[1] Across the country, some schools are digging up parts of their playgrounds to plant vegetables. Teachers say a garden can teach more than they expected.

[2] In science classes, students measure how fast plants grow, test the soil, and record how much water each bed needs. Lessons that once came only from a textbook now happen outdoors.

[3] The gardens also change what students eat. Teachers report that students who grow vegetables are much more willing to taste them, and some cafeterias now serve food from the school's own garden.

Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
check.hint: Write a few words for each paragraph. Which choice covers paragraphs 2 and 3 together?
check.explain: Paragraph 1 introduces the topic: a garden teaches more than expected. Paragraph 2 is about science lessons; paragraph 3 is about eating. The central idea must cover both: school gardens give hands-on science lessons and encourage healthier eating. The “textbooks” choice is tempting because it echoes paragraph 2, but it exaggerates what the passage says.
options: School gardens give students hands-on science lessons and encourage healthier eating.
Students in school gardens measure how fast plants grow.
Every school should replace part of its playground with a garden.
School gardens have replaced science textbooks.
why: This is a detail from paragraph 2 only. It is too narrow because it leaves out the change in eating habits.
This is not stated. The passage describes what some schools are doing; it never says every school should do it.
This is distorted. Paragraph 2 says lessons that once came only from a textbook now also happen outdoors. It never says textbooks were replaced.

screens.title: Supporting details
screens.html:
Supporting details explain, prove, or illustrate the main idea. Most fall into a few kinds:

KindExample
Fact or statisticHomes with shade used 12 percent less electricity.
ExampleLibraries help people write résumés.
ReasonWalking is easy on the knees.
Quotation“I came for the tomatoes,” said one gardener.
DescriptionThe sidewalk measured 131 degrees.

Writers often signal each new detail with words such as first, second, also, another, in addition, for example, and finally. Counting those signals is a quick way to see how a paragraph is built.

check.prompt:
“Our town should keep the public pool open all summer. First, it gives children a safe place to swim with a lifeguard on duty. Second, it offers free swim lessons, so more children learn to be safe around water. Third, it gives teenagers summer jobs.”

How many separate reasons does the writer give to support the main idea? Type a number.
check.hint: The first sentence is the claim. Count the sentences that give a reason for it.
check.explain: The first sentence is the main idea: the pool should stay open. The signal words First, Second, and Third each introduce one reason: a safe place to swim, free swim lessons, and summer jobs. Answer: 3.

mistakes.why: You counted the first sentence as a reason. The first sentence is the main idea (the claim); the reasons are the sentences that support it.
Count again: the signal words first, second, and third each introduce one reason.

screens.title: The umbrella test
screens.html:
Think of the main idea as an umbrella. Every important detail must fit under it.

  • If a statement covers only one or two details, the umbrella is too small. We call that too narrow.
  • If a statement covers much more than the text discusses, the umbrella is too big. We call that too broad.
  • A statement that covers all the details and nothing more is just right.

A too-narrow statement is usually true. That is why it is tempting. Being true is not enough; it must cover the whole text.

check.prompt:
Reread the bat paragraph: “Many people think of bats as frightening pests. In fact, bats are some of the most useful animals a farmer can have. Bats eat huge numbers of insects that damage crops. Some bats also pollinate plants, such as the agave. Farmers who protect bats often need less pesticide.”

Drag each statement into the correct category as a possible main idea of the paragraph.
check.hint: Ask of each statement: does it cover all three details, only one, or much more than the paragraph talks about?
check.explain:
Just right: “Bats are very useful animals for farmers” covers all three details (eating pests, pollinating, less pesticide).

Too narrow: the insect statement and the agave statement are each one detail.

Too broad: “All animals help people in some way” goes far beyond a paragraph about bats and farmers.
choices: Bats eat insects that damage crops.
Bats are very useful animals for farmers.
All animals help people in some way.
Some bats pollinate the agave plant.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting “Bats eat insects that damage crops” under Just right because it is true and important. It covers only one of the three ways bats help farmers, so it is too narrow.

screens.title: Choosing the detail that best supports a claim
screens.html:
Many GED questions ask, “Which detail best supports the idea that…?” Several choices will be true. Only one will prove that specific claim.

  1. Restate the claim in your own words.
  2. For each choice, ask: if this is true, does it prove the claim?
  3. Cross out details that are true but prove a different point, details that describe the problem instead of the result, and details that are only background.

example.prompt: Claim: “A credit score can affect much more than whether you get a loan.” Which detail best supports it: (1) Banks use credit scores to approve loans. (2) Landlords often check credit before renting an apartment.
steps: Restate: credit scores matter for things other than loans.
Detail 1 is about loans, the one thing the claim says to look beyond.
Detail 2 shows credit affecting housing, which is something other than a loan.

check.prompt:
Claim: “Remote work has helped the small town of Corbin grow.”

Which detail best supports this claim?
check.hint: The detail must connect remote work to growth in Corbin, not just mention one of them.
check.explain: The claim links two things: remote work and Corbin's growth. Only the “moved in for the low rents” choice connects them: remote workers moved in, and new shops filled most of the empty storefronts. The rents detail is tempting because it is related, but it does not show any change in Corbin.
options: Remote workers moved in for the low rents, and new shops filled most of the empty storefronts.
Many remote workers hold video meetings every day and rarely travel to a central office.
Rents in large cities are much higher than rents in small towns such as Corbin.
Ten years ago, six of the storefronts on Corbin's Main Street stood empty.
why: This is about how remote workers do their jobs. It says nothing about Corbin or any change there.
This explains why someone might move, but it does not show that anyone moved or that Corbin grew.
This describes the problem before remote workers arrived. It shows where Corbin started, not that it grew.

screens.title: Relevant and not relevant
screens.html:
A detail is relevant when it supports the main idea of its paragraph. On the GED, editing questions sometimes ask which sentence should be removed because it does not belong.

To find it, state the paragraph's main idea, then test each sentence: does this help prove or explain the main idea? The sentence that does not belong is often about the same general subject, which is what makes it tricky. It mentions the same place or thing, but it does not support the point.

check.prompt: Click the sentence that does not support the main idea of the paragraph.
check.hint: State the main idea first. Then find the sentence that is about the same street but not about safety.
check.explain: The main idea is the first sentence: the bike lanes have made cycling safer. Fewer crashes, posts that separate bikes from cars, and parents letting children ride all support it. “Grant Avenue was named after a former mayor” is about the same street, but it says nothing about safety, so it does not belong.
spans: The city's new bike lanes have made cycling safer on Grant Avenue.
Since the lanes opened, crashes involving cyclists on the avenue have dropped by half.
A row of plastic posts now separates bikes from car traffic.
Grant Avenue was named after a former mayor.
More parents now let their children ride bikes to school along the avenue.
check.why: Some readers click the sentence about plastic posts because it describes equipment rather than results. The posts are part of what makes the lanes safer, so that sentence belongs. The mayor sentence is about the street's name, not about safety.

screens.title: Implied main ideas
screens.html:
Sometimes no sentence states the main idea. The writer gives you the details and trusts you to see the point. Use these five steps:

  1. List the main details in a few words each.
  2. Ask: what do these details have in common?
  3. Ask: what does the author want me to understand?
  4. Write one complete sentence.
  5. Test it with the umbrella.

A helpful frame: “These details all show that ______.”

example.prompt: “In 2015, the town of Bellport had four grocery stores. Today it has one, on the far edge of town. Residents without cars now take two buses to reach it. Meanwhile, the number of convenience stores selling mostly packaged snacks has doubled. Fewer than half of Bellport families eat fresh vegetables on most days.”
steps: List: fewer grocery stores; the last one is far away; long bus trips; more snack shops; fewer families eat vegetables.
In common: getting healthy food has become hard.
Write and test: every detail fits under “healthy food is hard to get in Bellport.”
example.answer: Implied main idea: “The loss of grocery stores has made it hard for many Bellport residents to get fresh, healthy food.”

check.prompt:
“Three years ago, the Westside branch library began opening on Sundays. Sunday is now its busiest day of the week. The homework help table is full every Sunday afternoon. Parents who work weekday shifts say Sunday is the only day they can bring their children.”

Which statement best expresses the implied main idea?
check.hint: List the four details. What do they all show about the Sunday hours?
check.explain: List the details: Sunday hours began, Sunday is the busiest day, the homework table is full, and working parents can come only then. Together they show that Sunday hours filled a real need. The “only on Sundays” choice is tempting because it uses words from the paragraph, but it drops a key limit: “who work weekday shifts.”
options: Opening on Sundays has met a real need for Westside families.
The Westside library has a homework help table.
Every public library should be open seven days a week.
Parents can bring their children to the library only on Sundays.
why: This is one detail. It is too narrow because it leaves out the crowds and the working parents.
This is not stated. The paragraph is about one library; it never says what every library should do.
This is distorted. The paragraph says Sunday is the only day for parents who work weekday shifts, not for all parents.

screens.title: Proving an implied main idea
screens.html:
When the main idea is implied, you still need evidence. GED questions may tell you the implied idea and ask which details support it. The trick is to read the idea closely. If it says the mill closing hurt “more than its own workers,” then a detail about the mill's workers losing jobs does not prove it. You need details about other people or businesses.

Underline the key words in the idea you are proving. A detail must match those key words, not just the general topic.

check.prompt:
“When the Hartwell paper mill closed in 2019, 600 workers lost their jobs. Within a year, the diner across the street cut its hours. Two of the three gas stations in town closed. Enrollment at the elementary school fell as families moved away.”

The implied main idea is that the mill's closing hurt much more than the mill's own workers. Which two details support this idea? Select two answers.
check.hint: Underline “more than the mill's own workers.” Which details are about someone other than the mill's workers?
check.explain: The key words are “more than the mill's own workers.” The diner cutting hours and the gas stations closing show businesses outside the mill being hurt. (The school enrollment detail would also work, but it is not one of the choices.) The 600-jobs detail is the most tempting because it is the biggest number, but it is about the mill's own workers.
options: The diner across the street cut its hours.
Two of the three gas stations in town closed.
600 workers lost their jobs.
The mill closed in 2019.
Paper mills use large amounts of water.
why: This is about the mill's own workers. The idea is that the damage went beyond them, so this detail does not prove it.
This is the date of the closing. It tells when, not who else was hurt.
This is not in the paragraph at all, and it says nothing about who was hurt.

screens.title: What goes in a summary
screens.html:
A summary restates a text's central idea and key points in your own words. It is much shorter than the original. Five steps:

  1. State the central idea in one sentence.
  2. Add two to four key points, usually one for each major part.
  3. Leave out small examples, exact numbers, and quotations unless they are essential.
  4. Add nothing: no opinions, no facts from outside the text.
  5. Check every sentence against the text.

Cover the text and write your summary from memory. Then uncover it and check. This keeps you from copying sentences and shows what you really understood.

check.prompt: Which two things do not belong in a summary? Select two answers.
check.hint: A summary reports what the text says, briefly. What would add to the text or clutter it?
check.explain: A summary includes the central idea and key points, in your own words. It leaves out your opinions (a summary is objective) and minor details such as a hook story, small examples, and most numbers or quotations.
options: The central idea of the text
The key point of each major section
Your opinion of the topic
A minor example, such as one person's story used as a hook
Your own words instead of copied sentences
why: Every summary must include the central idea. It is the first thing you write.
Key points from each major section are the body of a summary. Leaving them out makes a summary too narrow.
Using your own words is required in a summary, not something to leave out.

screens.title: Choosing the best summary
screens.html:
On the GED you will more often choose a summary than write one. Test each choice with three questions:

  1. Coverage: does it include the central idea and the key points of every major part?
  2. Accuracy: is every fact correct, with nothing changed or exaggerated?
  3. Objectivity: is it free of opinions and outside information?

The best summary passes all three. A choice that copies one striking detail fails coverage. A choice that sounds complete but swaps a fact fails accuracy. A choice that says what “should” happen usually fails objectivity.

check.prompt:
“Many cities are replacing old streetlights with LED lights. LEDs use much less electricity than older lights, and they last for many years, so crews replace them less often. Some residents complained that the first LEDs were too bright and bluish. In response, many cities switched to warmer, dimmer LEDs.”

Which is the best summary of the paragraph?
check.hint: Check each choice for coverage, accuracy, and opinion.
check.explain: The paragraph has two parts: why cities are switching (energy, long life) and how they responded to complaints (warmer, dimmer LEDs). The “save energy and upkeep” choice covers both accurately with no opinion. The “taking down” choice is tempting because complaints are mentioned, but it reverses what the cities did.
options: Cities are switching to LED streetlights to save energy and upkeep, and many adjusted the lights after complaints.
LED streetlights use much less electricity than older lights.
LED lights are the best invention of the century, and every home should use them.
Cities are taking down their new LED streetlights and putting the older lights back up because residents said the LEDs were too bright.
why: This is accurate but too narrow. It leaves out how long LEDs last and the complaints that led to warmer lights.
This adds opinions (“best invention,” “every home should”) that the paragraph never states.
This is distorted. Cities did not take down LEDs or bring back the old lights; they switched to warmer, dimmer LEDs.

screens.title: The four answer traps
screens.html:
Wrong answers on main idea and summary questions are written to sound right. Almost all of them fall into four traps:

TrapWhat it looks likeAsk yourself
Too narrowA true detail from one part of the textDoes it cover the whole text?
Too broadA big statement, bigger than the textDoes the text really discuss all of this?
Not statedAn opinion or outside factCan I point to where it says this?
DistortedA detail that is changed, reversed, or exaggeratedDoes it match the text exactly in meaning?

Naming the trap on every wrong choice makes you faster and surer. It also tells you which skill to practice when you miss a question.

check.prompt:
“The Eastside Farmers Market began accepting SNAP food benefits two years ago. Since then, the number of shoppers has nearly doubled, and several farmers have added a second weekly market day. Market managers say many new shoppers had never been able to buy produce from local farms before.”

Each statement below is a wrong answer to “What is the main idea?” Name the trap.

“Several farmers have added a second weekly market day.” {{0}}

“Every farmers market in the country should accept SNAP.” {{1}}

“The number of shoppers has tripled since the market began accepting SNAP.” {{2}}
check.hint: Compare each statement with the paragraph. Is it true but small, missing from the text, or a real detail that has been changed?
check.explain:
Statement 1 is true but covers only one detail: too narrow.

Statement 2 is an opinion about every market that the paragraph never gives: not stated.

Statement 3 takes a real detail (“nearly doubled”) and changes it (“tripled”): distorted.

The main idea itself would be: accepting SNAP has brought many new shoppers to the market and helped local farmers grow.

options: too narrow
too broad
not stated
distorted
why: Too broad means bigger than the text. This statement is smaller than the text: it is one true detail.
This is stated; it is the second half of sentence 2. The problem is that it covers only one detail.
Nothing is changed here; the statement matches the paragraph exactly. It is simply only one detail.

options: too narrow
not stated
distorted
why: Too narrow means a true detail from the text. This statement does not appear in the text at all.
Distorted means a real detail that has been changed. The paragraph contains no statement about other markets to change; this is an added opinion.

options: too narrow
too broad
distorted
why: Too narrow means a true detail. This statement is not true to the text, which says shoppers nearly doubled.
Too broad means bigger than the text. This statement is about this one market; its problem is a changed number.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • The topic is a word or phrase. The main idea (or central idea for a passage) is a complete sentence that can be true or false.
  • Main ideas often come first, but watch for hooks and turns (however, in fact, but), main ideas at the end, and implied main ideas.
  • Supporting details are facts, numbers, examples, reasons, and quotations. The best support proves the exact claim in the question.
  • Use the umbrella test: the main idea covers every important detail, and no more.
  • A summary gives the central idea and key points, in your own words, with no opinions and no minor details.
  • Name the trap on every wrong answer: too narrow, too broad, not stated, distorted.
  • On test day: predict the answer in your own words, match it to a choice, and test it.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Shade Is Infrastructure: Why Cities Are Counting Their Trees
stimuli.html:
[1] On a July afternoon in Marlow Falls, a sidewalk in the Eastgate neighborhood measured 131 degrees Fahrenheit. Two miles away, on a tree-lined street in the Hillcrest neighborhood, the same kind of sidewalk measured 94 degrees. The air temperature in both places was almost the same. The difference was shade. For decades, trees were treated as decoration, something to add after the “real” work of paving roads and laying pipes was done. Now a growing number of planners argue that trees are infrastructure: public equipment that a city needs in order to work, just like streetlights and storm drains.

[2] The most obvious service trees provide is cooling. Surfaces that stay out of direct sun absorb far less heat. When the walls and roof of a house stay cooler, the air conditioner inside does not have to run as long. In a study by the Marlow Falls electric utility, homes with mature trees shading their south and west sides used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling over one summer than similar homes without shade. Trees also release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air, much as sweat cools skin.

[3] Cooling is only part of the story, however. Trees also help cities manage rain. During a storm, leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall, and roots draw water down into the soil instead of letting it race across pavement. That matters because nearly every gallon that runs off a street ends up in the city's storm drains. When too much water arrives at once, the drains overflow and streets flood. Marlow Falls engineers estimate that the city's existing trees hold back enough runoff to delay a planned $40 million expansion of the drainage system by at least ten years.

[4] Shade also protects people. Heat kills more people in the United States than any other type of weather. Doctors at Marlow Falls General Hospital reported that most emergency visits for heat illness during last summer's heat waves came from the city's three least-shaded neighborhoods.

[5] The trouble is that these benefits are not shared equally. When Marlow Falls completed its first full tree count in 2023, it found that trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate. Older, wealthier neighborhoods often have large trees planted generations ago, while neighborhoods built near highways, factories, or large parking lots have few. The residents with the least shade are frequently the ones who can least afford high cooling bills.

[6] To close that gap, Marlow Falls adopted a plan last year to plant 15,000 trees over the next ten years, with most of them going to neighborhoods where tree cover is below 20 percent. Young trees need regular watering for their first three years, and many die without it. So the city is hiring and training local residents to care for new trees on their own blocks.

stimuli.title: Draft Memo: Study Hall Is Moving
stimuli.html:
To: Evening Study Hall Volunteers
From: Renee Alvarez, Adult Learning Coordinator
Date: February 14
Subject: Study hall is moving to Room 112

(1) Starting Monday, March 3, our Tuesday and Thursday evening study hall will move from the library annex to Room 112 in the main building. The hours will stay the same, 6:00 to 8:30 p.m. In this memo, I want to explain the reasons for the move and what it will mean for you as a volunteer tutor.

(2) (A) Room 112 seats thirty people, compared with fifteen in the annex, so we will no longer have to turn learners away on busy nights. It also has twelve laptops that learners can use for online practice tests. The room is next to the east parking lot, which matters to learners who come straight from work and arrive just as study hall begins. The annex will be repainted next summer. Finally, the room has a whiteboard wall where tutors can work through problems with small groups.

(3) The move does come with one new responsibility. Because Room 112 is shared with a daytime English class, we must leave it exactly as we found it. Each volunteer (B) asked to arrive ten minutes early to set up the laptops and to return all materials to the supply cabinet before leaving. Please also make sure the laptops are plugged into the charging cart at the end of the evening so they are ready for the morning class.

(4) Learners will receive a printed notice about the new room during the last week of February, and signs in the annex will direct anyone who forgets. If a learner shows up at the annex during the first few weeks, please walk with that person to Room 112 so no one misses study time.

(5) Thank you for your flexibility. Many of our learners have told me that study hall is the most useful part of their week, and that is because of you. If you have questions about the move, please call me at extension 214 or stop by my office before March 3.

stimuli.title: Lights Out for Hatchlings
stimuli.html:
[1] On summer nights along the beaches of Pine Key, sea turtle hatchlings dig their way out of nests buried in the sand. Within minutes, they begin crawling toward the water. Scientists have found that hatchlings find the ocean mainly by moving toward the brightest part of the horizon. On a natural beach, that is the open sky over the sea, which reflects moonlight and starlight.

[2] For decades, the beachfront on Pine Key was lined with hotels, condominiums, and streetlights. Their lights shone brighter than the sky over the water. Volunteers who checked nests each morning often found tiny tracks leading away from the ocean, toward parking lots and roads. In 2015, volunteers recorded 212 nests where hatchlings had crawled in the wrong direction.

[3] Late that year, the county passed a lighting rule for beachfront property. Lights that can be seen from the beach must now be shielded, mounted low, and fitted with amber or red bulbs, colors that turtles have trouble seeing. Hotels hung darker curtains on ocean-facing windows, and the county replaced 300 streetlights along the beach road. Some property owners complained about the cost, so the county offered small grants to help them pay for new fixtures.

[4] Volunteers still check every nest each morning. Last season, they recorded only 31 nests where hatchlings crawled the wrong way, even though the total number of nests on the beach was about the same as in 2015. Volunteers say the beach road, once bright all night, now looks almost dark from the sand.

stimuli.title: Sleep on It: How Rest Helps the Brain Learn
stimuli.html:
[1] At 2 a.m., Luis is still at his kitchen table with a stack of flash cards. His GED Science test is in eight hours, and he has decided that every hour of sleep he skips is another hour of studying. Many test-takers make the same choice. A large body of research suggests, however, that Luis has the trade-off backward. Sleep is not time stolen from learning. It is one of the times when learning actually happens.

[2] For much of history, people assumed that sleep was simply the brain switching off. That idea began to fall apart in the twentieth century, when scientists started recording the electrical activity of sleeping brains. The recordings showed that the brain stays busy all night. It moves through a repeating cycle of stages, including light sleep, deep sleep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, completing one cycle about every 90 minutes.

[3] One of the sleeping brain's most important jobs is protecting new memories. When you learn something during the day, such as a new vocabulary word or the steps of a math problem, the memory is first held in a part of the brain called the hippocampus. This storage is temporary and fragile, like a document that has been typed but not yet saved. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay the day's new information and strengthen it, moving it into longer-term storage in the brain's outer layer, the cortex.

[4] Experiments support this idea. In one study, volunteers learned a list of forty word pairs, such as “ocean–lamp,” in the evening. Half of the group then slept for eight hours. The other half stayed awake for the same eight hours. When both groups were tested afterward, the people who had slept remembered about 20 percent more word pairs than those who had stayed awake. Researchers have repeated versions of this experiment many times with similar results: people who sleep after learning tend to remember more than people who do not.

[5] Different stages of sleep may help with different kinds of learning. Deep sleep, which is most common early in the night, appears especially important for facts, such as dates, definitions, and formulas. REM sleep, which grows longer in the early-morning hours, seems to help the brain connect ideas and practice skills. This is one reason a short night can be so costly: someone who sleeps only four hours misses much of the REM sleep that normally comes in the final hours of a full night.

[6] For learners, the message is practical. Studying and then sleeping is a better plan than studying all night. A short review of key material in the evening, followed by a full night of rest, gives the brain a chance to do its overnight work. Luis would likely remember more if he put down the flash cards, went to bed, and spent ten minutes reviewing them in the morning. Sleep is not a break from studying. It is part of studying.

stimuli.title: Draft Memo: A New Way to Swap Shifts
stimuli.html:
To: All Staff, Fresh Market on Elm
From: Denise Carter, Store Manager
Date: March 10
Subject: Shift swaps are moving to the scheduling app

(1) Starting April 1, all shift swaps will be requested through the store's scheduling app instead of the paper binder in the break room. This memo explains why we are making the change and how the new system will work.

(2) (A) Requests written in the binder were sometimes missed because managers did not check it every day. Some pages were torn out or became hard to read after spills. Last month, two employees showed up for the same shift because a swap was never recorded. The break room will get a new refrigerator in May. Finally, employees who were not at the store could not see which shifts were open.

(3) The app fixes these problems. To request a swap, open the app, tap the shift you need covered, and choose a coworker who is available. Your coworker will get a message and can accept with one tap. Each of the requests (B) reviewed by a manager within one business day, and you will get a notice as soon as your swap is approved. Because the schedule lives in the app, you can check open shifts from anywhere.

(4) Training will be held in the break room on March 24 and March 26 at 2:00 p.m. A printed step-by-step guide will be posted next to the time clock. If you need help setting up the app on your phone, assistant manager Jamal Pierce can walk you through it during any shift.

(5) Thank you for your patience as we make this change. A schedule that everyone can see and trust makes every shift run more smoothly.

stimuli.title: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.html:
[1] During and after World War I, wheat prices were high, and the southern Great Plains enjoyed several wet years. Farmers in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado, and New Mexico used new gasoline tractors to plow up millions of acres of native prairie grass and plant wheat. Those grasses had deep, tangled roots that had held the soil in place through dry spells and strong winds for thousands of years.

[2] Then, in the early 1930s, a long drought began. Crops withered, and the plowed fields were left bare. The region's strong winds picked up the dry topsoil and carried it away in enormous clouds. Some storms, which people called “black blizzards,” turned day into night. On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as “Black Sunday,” one massive storm swept across the plains. During the worst years, dust from the region drifted as far as the East Coast.

[3] Families hung wet sheets over their windows to keep the dust out, but it still coated their food and furniture. Many people developed a lung illness that doctors called “dust pneumonia.” Hundreds of thousands of people left the plains during the 1930s, many heading west to California in search of work.

[4] In 1935, Congress created the Soil Conservation Service. Its experts taught farmers to plow along the curves of the land instead of in straight lines, to rotate crops, and to leave some fields covered with grass. The government also paid to plant long rows of trees, called shelterbelts, to slow the wind. When steady rains returned around 1940, these methods helped keep the soil in place.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.hint: Find the choice that fits over every paragraph, not just one. Paragraph 1 ends with the author's big claim.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the author's central claim. Paragraph 1 ends: planners “argue that trees are infrastructure: public equipment that a city needs in order to work.”

Step 2. Check the rest of the passage. Paragraphs 2–4 describe benefits (cooling, managing rain, protecting health). Paragraphs 5–6 explain that the benefits are unequal and describe the plan to plant trees where cover is low.

Step 3. Umbrella test: only the infrastructure choice covers all six paragraphs. The sidewalk choice is the most tempting because it comes first in the passage, but it is one detail, so it is too narrow.
options: Cities increasingly treat trees as infrastructure because trees deliver real benefits, and some aim to share them fairly.
On a July afternoon, an unshaded sidewalk in Eastgate measured 131 degrees, while a shaded one in Hillcrest measured 94.
Planting trees is a cheaper way to prevent flooding than expanding storm drains, so Marlow Falls has canceled its planned $40 million drainage expansion.
Wealthy neighborhoods such as Hillcrest should pay to plant and water new trees in neighborhoods such as Eastgate that have fewer of them.
why: This is a true detail from paragraph 1, but it is too narrow. It says nothing about rain, health, unequal tree cover, or the planting plan.
This is distorted. Paragraph 3 says trees may delay the drainage expansion by at least ten years, not that it was canceled or that trees are a cheaper replacement. It also covers only one paragraph.
This is not stated. The passage never says who should pay. It is an opinion a reader might add.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 2, how do shade trees reduce the amount of electricity a home uses?
items.hint: Paragraph 2 describes more than one way trees cool things. Which one is connected to what happens inside a house?
items.explain:
Step 1. Go to paragraph 2. It says that surfaces out of direct sun “absorb far less heat.”

Step 2. The next sentence connects this to electricity: “When the walls and roof of a house stay cooler, the air conditioner inside does not have to run as long.” That matches the walls-and-roof choice.

The water vapor choice is tempting because vapor is mentioned in the same paragraph, but the passage says it cools the outdoor air, not that it is piped inside.
options: They keep the home's walls and roof cooler, so the air conditioner does not have to run as long.
They block cold winds, so the home's heater does not have to run as long.
They release water vapor that is collected and piped into the home to cool it.
They lower the price that the utility company charges for electricity.
why: This is not stated. Paragraph 2 is about summer cooling; the passage never mentions winter, wind, or heaters.
This is distorted. Paragraph 2 says water vapor cools “the surrounding air.” Nothing is collected or piped indoors.
This is not stated. The homes used less electricity, but the passage never says the price of electricity changed.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 3 that best states the main idea of that paragraph.
items.hint: The first sentence links back to paragraph 2. Which sentence introduces the new point that the rest of the paragraph explains?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify what the paragraph is about. Every sentence after the first two is about rain: catching rainwater, runoff, overflowing drains, and the drainage expansion.

Step 2. Find the sentence that covers all of those details: “Trees also help cities manage rain.”

Step 3. Check the trap. “Cooling is only part of the story, however” is a transition. It connects to the cooling topic of paragraph 2 but does not say what this paragraph is about. The $40 million estimate is one piece of evidence, so it is too narrow.
spans: Cooling is only part of the story, however.
Trees also help cities manage rain.
During a storm, leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall, and roots draw water down into the soil instead of letting it race across pavement.
That matters because nearly every gallon that runs off a street ends up in the city's storm drains.
When too much water arrives at once, the drains overflow and streets flood.
Marlow Falls engineers estimate that the city's existing trees hold back enough runoff to delay a planned $40 million expansion of the drainage system by at least ten years.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the first sentence. “Cooling is only part of the story, however” is a transition that links back to paragraph 2; it does not say what paragraph 3 is about. The later sentences are details about rain, so they are too narrow.

items.prompt:
Read the draft memo. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): {{0}} Room 112 seats thirty people, compared with fifteen in the annex, so we will no longer have to turn learners away on busy nights.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): Each volunteer {{1}} asked to arrive ten minutes early to set up the laptops and to return all materials to the supply cabinet before leaving.
items.hint: For (A), read the rest of paragraph 2 and ask what all of its details describe. For (B), find the subject and decide whether it is singular or plural.
items.explain:
Blank (A). List what the rest of paragraph 2 describes: more seats, laptops, a location near parking, and a whiteboard wall. Every one is a reason Room 112 is better than the annex, so the topic sentence must say that: “The new room offers several advantages over the annex.” The other sentences are off topic.

Blank (B). The subject is “Each volunteer.” Each refers to one person at a time, so the subject is singular, and the memo is in the present tense. The verb must be singular and present: “Each volunteer is asked.” “Are” is the most tempting wrong answer, but it is plural.

options: The new room offers several advantages over the annex.
The library annex was built more than forty years ago.
Many of our volunteers are retired teachers.
Please remember to sign in at the front desk each evening.
why: This is about the annex's age, but paragraph 2 lists reasons Room 112 is better. A topic sentence must cover the details that follow it.
This is about the volunteers' backgrounds, which paragraph 2 never discusses. It does not cover the seats, laptops, parking, or whiteboard.
This is an instruction, not a main idea, and it has nothing to do with the room's features.

options: is
are
were
being
why: “Are” is plural. The subject is “Each volunteer,” and each means one person at a time, so the verb must be singular.
“Were” is plural and past tense. The subject is singular, and the memo describes what will happen, in the present tense.
“Being” cannot be the main verb of a sentence. “Each volunteer being asked…” is a fragment.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author states that the benefits of trees “are not shared equally.” Which detail from the passage best supports this statement?
items.hint: Look for a detail that compares two groups of people or places.
items.explain:
Step 1. Restate the claim: some places get more of the benefits of trees than others.

Step 2. To support it, a detail must compare places. “Trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate” shows exactly that difference.
