Step 3. The other details are true but support different points. The 12 percent electricity detail is the most tempting because it contains a number, but it proves that trees save energy, not that the savings are unequal.
options: “trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate”
“Young trees need regular watering for their first three years, and many die without it.”
“homes with mature trees shading their south and west sides used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling”
“leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall”
why: This detail explains why young trees need care (paragraph 6). It does not compare who has trees and who does not.
This detail shows that trees save energy (paragraph 2), not that some neighborhoods get more of that benefit than others.
This detail explains how trees manage storms (paragraph 3). It says nothing about unequal benefits.

items.prompt: The author suggests that trees can save money for residents and for the city. Which two details support this idea? Select two answers.
items.hint: Look for details that mention lower bills or costs that are avoided or put off.
items.explain:
Step 1. Look for details about money: lower bills or avoided costs.

Step 2. Using 12 percent less electricity for cooling means lower electric bills for residents (paragraph 2). Delaying a $40 million drainage expansion by at least ten years puts off a large cost for the city (paragraph 3).

Step 3. The sidewalk temperatures show heat, not money. The 41 percent and 9 percent figures show unequal tree cover. The watering and planting details describe the city's plan; they say nothing about savings.
options: Homes shaded by mature trees used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling over one summer.
The city's existing trees hold back enough runoff to delay a planned $40 million drainage expansion by at least ten years.
A sidewalk in Eastgate measured 131 degrees, while one in Hillcrest measured 94 degrees.
Trees covered 41 percent of Hillcrest but only 9 percent of Eastgate.
Young trees need regular watering for their first three years.
Marlow Falls plans to plant 15,000 trees over the next ten years.
why: This shows a difference in heat, not in money. Hot sidewalks do not, by themselves, show any cost or saving.
This shows unequal tree cover. It supports the idea that benefits are not shared equally, not the idea of saving money.
This describes a cost of caring for trees, not a saving.
This describes the city's plan. It says nothing about money saved.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 6, most of the new trees will go to neighborhoods where tree cover is below what percent? Type the number.
items.hint: Find the sentence in paragraph 6 that describes where the trees will be planted.
items.explain:
Step 1. Go to paragraph 6, where the plan is described.

Step 2. Find the sentence about where trees will go: “with most of them going to neighborhoods where tree cover is below 20 percent.”

Answer: 20. The numbers 41 and 9 appear in paragraph 5, but they describe two specific neighborhoods, not the plan's rule.

mistakes.why: 41 percent is Hillcrest's tree cover from paragraph 5. The plan's cutoff is stated in paragraph 6: neighborhoods “where tree cover is below 20 percent.”
9 percent is Eastgate's tree cover from paragraph 5. The question asks for the cutoff the plan uses, which is in paragraph 6.
15,000 is the number of trees the city plans to plant, not a percent. Look for “percent” in paragraph 6.

items.prompt: Which sentence should be removed from paragraph 2 of the memo because it does not support the main idea of the paragraph?
items.hint: Paragraph 2 is about why Room 112 is a better place for study hall. Which sentence is not about Room 112 at all?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the paragraph's main idea: Room 112 has advantages over the annex.

Step 2. Test each sentence. More seats, laptops, parking, whiteboard: each is an advantage of Room 112.

Step 3. “The annex will be repainted next summer” is about the old space and a future project. It gives no reason Room 112 is better, so it is not relevant. Some readers keep it because it mentions the annex, which the paragraph compares with Room 112, but this sentence makes no comparison at all.
options: Room 112 seats thirty people, compared with fifteen in the annex, so we will no longer have to turn learners away on busy nights.
It also has twelve laptops that learners can use for online practice tests.
The annex will be repainted next summer.
Finally, the room has a whiteboard wall where tutors can work through problems with small groups.
why: This is an advantage of Room 112 (more seats), so it supports the paragraph's main idea and should stay.
Laptops for practice tests are an advantage of Room 112, so this sentence belongs.
The whiteboard wall is another advantage of Room 112. “Finally” signals the last item in the list of advantages, so it belongs.

items.prompt: Which choice is the best summary of the passage?
items.hint: A good summary is accurate, covers the whole passage, and contains no opinions.
items.explain:
Step 1. A summary must give the central idea, cover the key points of every major section, be accurate, and stay objective.

Step 2. The “Planners now see trees as city infrastructure” choice states the central idea (trees as infrastructure), the benefits from paragraphs 2–4, the unequal coverage from paragraph 5, and the plan from paragraph 6. Every statement matches the text.

Step 3. The Hillcrest choice is the most tempting because it sounds complete, but it reverses the two neighborhoods, so it is distorted.
options: Planners now see trees as city infrastructure: they cool homes and streets, cut energy use, absorb stormwater, and protect health. Because tree cover is uneven, Marlow Falls plans to plant 15,000 trees, mostly in low-shade areas, and train residents to care for them.
Trees are the most important part of any city. Every city should follow the example of Marlow Falls and plant thousands of trees, because nothing else does as much to keep people healthy.
In Marlow Falls, a sidewalk in Eastgate reached 131 degrees while one in Hillcrest reached 94 degrees. Trees release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the air much as sweat cools skin.

Trees cool streets, lower electric bills, absorb rain, and reduce heat illness. Because Hillcrest has far less tree cover than Eastgate, Marlow Falls plans to plant 15,000 trees in Hillcrest over the next ten years and is hiring Hillcrest residents to water the young trees.
why: This adds opinions (“most important part of any city,” “every city should”) that the author never states. A summary must be objective.
This is too narrow. It repeats two details from paragraphs 1 and 2 and leaves out rain, health, unequal cover, and the plan.
This is distorted. Paragraph 5 says Hillcrest has more tree cover (41 percent) than Eastgate (9 percent), and the plan targets neighborhoods with low cover, not Hillcrest.

items.prompt:
Renee wants to add a sentence at the beginning of paragraph 4 of the memo that states the paragraph's main idea. Which sentence works best?

{{0}} Learners will receive a printed notice about the new room during the last week of February, and signs in the annex will direct anyone who forgets.
items.hint: List what paragraph 4 describes. What do all of those details have in common?
items.explain:
Step 1. List the details in paragraph 4: a printed notice, signs in the annex, and volunteers walking lost learners to Room 112.

Step 2. Ask what they have in common: each one helps learners find the new room.

Step 3. The topic sentence must cover all of them: “We have a plan to make sure learners can find the new room.” The laptop sentence is tempting because it is about Room 112, but it belongs to paragraph 2.

options: We have a plan to make sure learners can find the new room.
The annex has served our program well for many years.
Room 112 has twelve laptops for online practice tests.
Some learners may decide to stop coming to study hall.
why: Paragraph 4 is not about the annex's history. Its details (printed notices, signs, walking learners over) are all ways to help learners find Room 112.
This is a detail from paragraph 2. It has nothing to do with notices, signs, or walking learners to the new room.
This is not stated anywhere in the memo, and it does not cover the details in paragraph 4.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the memo.

The main purpose of the memo is to {{0}}. The detail that best supports the claim that the move will help learners is that {{1}}.
items.hint: For the first blank, reread the last sentence of paragraph 1. For the second, look for a change that makes things better for learners, not for volunteers.
items.explain:
Blank 1. Paragraph 1 says the memo will “explain the reasons for the move and what it will mean for you as a volunteer tutor.” Paragraphs 2–4 do exactly that, so the purpose is to explain the move and what it means for volunteers. The laptop and thank-you choices each describe only one paragraph.

Blank 2. The claim is that the move helps learners, so the detail must show an improvement for learners. Thirty seats instead of fifteen means learners will no longer be turned away. The unchanged hours are tempting, but staying the same is not an improvement.

options: explain the move to Room 112 and what it means for volunteers
describe the laptops that learners can use in Room 112
thank volunteers for their flexibility
convince volunteers to help repaint the annex
why: This is too narrow. The laptops are one detail in paragraph 2, not the purpose of the whole memo.
This is too narrow. Thanks appear only in the closing paragraph; most of the memo explains the move.
This is distorted. The memo mentions that the annex will be repainted, but it never asks volunteers to help.

options: Room 112 seats thirty, so learners will no longer be turned away
the room is shared with a daytime English class
volunteers must arrive ten minutes early
the hours will stay the same
why: This explains a new responsibility for volunteers. It does not show any benefit for learners.
This is a duty for volunteers, not a benefit for learners.
This shows that something stays the same. A detail that proves the move helps must show an improvement.

items.skill: How a paragraph develops the central idea
items.prompt: How does paragraph 5 contribute to the development of the central idea of the passage?
items.hint: Look at the first words of paragraph 5 and the first words of paragraph 6. How are they connected?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the first sentence of paragraph 5: “The trouble is that these benefits are not shared equally.” “The trouble” signals a problem.

Step 2. The rest of the paragraph proves the problem (41 percent versus 9 percent) and explains why it matters (people with the least shade can least afford cooling bills).

Step 3. Paragraph 6 begins, “To close that gap,” so paragraph 5 sets up the problem the plan solves. The cooling-cost choice is tempting because paragraph 5 mentions cooling bills, but that is not the paragraph's job.
options: It shows that tree cover is uneven, setting up the problem that the plan in paragraph 6 is meant to solve.
It gives more evidence that shade trees lower the cost of cooling a home, adding to the electricity study in paragraph 2.
It argues that wealthy neighborhoods such as Hillcrest should give some of their trees to poorer neighborhoods such as Eastgate.
It explains how trees keep storm drains from overflowing during heavy rain.
why: This is distorted. Paragraph 5 mentions cooling bills, but its new information is about who has trees, not more proof that shade saves money; it reports no new study.
This is not stated. Paragraph 5 describes the difference between neighborhoods; it never says trees should be moved or given away.
This describes paragraph 3, not paragraph 5.

items.prompt: The author does not state the central idea in one sentence. Which statement best expresses the implied central idea of the passage?
items.hint: List what each paragraph tells you, then ask what the numbers in paragraphs 2 and 4 show when you put them side by side.
items.explain:
Step 1. List the main details: hatchlings move toward the brightest horizon (paragraph 1); bright beachfront lights sent many the wrong way, 212 nests in 2015 (paragraph 2); a lighting rule changed the lights (paragraph 3); only 31 nests had lost hatchlings last season (paragraph 4).

Step 2. Ask what they add up to: changing the lights helped the hatchlings.

Step 3. Umbrella test: the “Changing the lights” choice covers every paragraph. The “no hatchlings” choice is the most tempting because it sounds like the happy ending, but it exaggerates the result.
options: Changing the lights along the beachfront has helped far more Pine Key hatchlings head toward the ocean.
The county replaced 300 streetlights along the beach road.
Human activity is harming wildlife all over the world.
Since the lighting rule passed, no hatchlings on Pine Key crawl the wrong way.
why: This is too narrow. It is one detail from paragraph 3 and says nothing about why lights matter or what happened to the hatchlings.
This is too broad. The passage is about one beach and one problem, lighting, not all wildlife everywhere.
This is distorted. Paragraph 4 says 31 nests still had hatchlings crawl the wrong way. The problem shrank; it did not disappear.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category based on the passage.
items.hint: For each statement, try to point to the exact sentence that says it. If you cannot find one, where does it go?
items.explain:
Central idea: “Changes to beachfront lighting have helped more hatchlings reach the sea.” It covers all four paragraphs.

Supporting details: The brightest-horizon fact (paragraph 1) explains why lights matter. The 212 nests (paragraph 2) shows how bad the problem was.

Not in the passage: The passage never discusses turtles returning to lay eggs. It also never says most hotel owners supported the rule; it says some owners complained about the cost. If you cannot point to it in the text, it is not in the passage.
choices: Changes to beachfront lighting have helped more hatchlings reach the sea.
Hatchlings find the ocean mainly by moving toward the brightest part of the horizon.
In 2015, volunteers recorded 212 nests where hatchlings crawled the wrong way.
Sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
Most hotel owners supported the lighting rule from the start.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the statement about sea turtles returning to their home beach under “Supporting detail” because it sounds like a real fact. It may be true, but the passage never says it, so it is not in the passage. The hotel statement is also not in the passage; paragraph 3 says only that some owners complained about the cost.

items.prompt: Which choice is the best summary of the passage?
items.hint: Check each choice for three things: does it cover the whole passage, is every fact accurate, and is it free of opinion?
items.explain:
Step 1. A strong summary gives the central idea and the key point of each part: the cause (hatchlings follow light), the problem (bright lights, 212 nests), the response (the lighting rule), and the result (31 nests).

Step 2. The “212 to 31” choice includes all four, accurately and without opinion. Here the two numbers are worth keeping because they are the result.

Step 3. The “banned all lights” choice is tempting because it sounds like a clear cause and effect, but its key facts are wrong.
options: Hatchlings head for the brightest horizon, so Pine Key's beachfront lights once misled many. After a rule required shielded, low, amber or red lights, nests with lost hatchlings fell from 212 to 31.
Volunteers on Pine Key check every sea turtle nest each morning and record what they find.
Pine Key's lighting rule is unfair to property owners, who should not have to pay for new lights to protect turtles.

After the county banned all lights near the beach and hotels hung darker curtains, the number of sea turtle nests on Pine Key grew sharply, and volunteers no longer need to check the nests each morning.
why: This is too narrow. It describes the volunteers' routine but leaves out the lights, the rule, and the result.
This adds an opinion the author never gives. A summary must be objective; the passage only reports that some owners complained.

This is distorted in three ways. The rule required shielded, low, amber or red lights; it did not ban all lights. Paragraph 4 says the total number of nests stayed about the same. And volunteers still check every nest each morning.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.hint: Look at how paragraph 1 and paragraph 6 end. Then check which choice fits every paragraph in between.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the stated claim. Paragraph 1 ends: “Sleep is not time stolen from learning. It is one of the times when learning actually happens.” Paragraph 6 ends: “Sleep is not a break from studying. It is part of studying.”

Step 2. Check the middle. Paragraph 2 shows the brain is busy during sleep; paragraph 3 explains how sleep strengthens memories; paragraph 4 gives experimental evidence; paragraph 5 explains how different stages help; paragraph 6 gives advice. The “Sleep is an active process” choice covers all of this.

Step 3. The 90-minute choice is tempting because it is accurate, but it is only one detail.
options: Sleep is an active process that helps the brain strengthen and store new learning, so it is an important part of studying.
The sleeping brain moves through light sleep, deep sleep, and REM sleep about every 90 minutes.
Test-takers should never review any material in the evening and should instead save all of their studying for the morning of the test.
Scientists have not yet found any clear connection between sleep and memory, so the advice to sleep before a test is still only a guess.
why: This is a true detail from paragraph 2, but it is too narrow. It says nothing about memory, the research, or the advice to learners.
This is distorted. Paragraph 6 actually recommends “a short review of key material in the evening,” followed by a brief review in the morning, not saving all studying for the morning.
This contradicts the passage. Paragraphs 3 and 4 describe exactly that connection and the experiments that support it.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 3, where is a new memory held first, before sleep strengthens it?
items.hint: Paragraph 3 names two parts of the brain. Which one comes first?
items.explain:
Step 1. Go to paragraph 3. The second sentence says the memory “is first held in a part of the brain called the hippocampus.”

Step 2. The last sentence says that during deep sleep the memory moves “into longer-term storage in the brain's outer layer, the cortex.”

So the first stop is the hippocampus. The cortex is the most tempting wrong answer because it is named in the same paragraph, but it is the second stop.
options: In a part of the brain called the hippocampus
In the brain's outer layer, the cortex
In a document that has been typed but not saved
In the part of the brain that controls REM sleep
why: This is distorted. The cortex is where the memory moves after it is strengthened during deep sleep, not where it starts.
This takes a comparison literally. The author compares fragile memory storage to an unsaved document; no real document is involved.
This is not stated. The passage never names a part of the brain that controls REM sleep.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 5 that best states the main idea of that paragraph.
items.hint: Two sentences each describe one stage of sleep. Which sentence covers both of them?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the whole paragraph. It describes deep sleep (facts) and REM sleep (connecting ideas and skills), then explains why a short night is costly.

Step 2. Find the sentence that covers both stages: “Different stages of sleep may help with different kinds of learning.” The two middle sentences are the two examples.

Step 3. The last sentence is a consequence of the REM detail only, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.
spans: Different stages of sleep may help with different kinds of learning.
Deep sleep, which is most common early in the night, appears especially important for facts, such as dates, definitions, and formulas.
REM sleep, which grows longer in the early-morning hours, seems to help the brain connect ideas and practice skills.
This is one reason a short night can be so costly: someone who sleeps only four hours misses much of the REM sleep that normally comes in the final hours of a full night.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the last sentence, because it sounds like a conclusion. It is actually a result of the REM detail, so it covers only part of the paragraph. The deep sleep and REM sentences are each one example of the first sentence's idea.

items.prompt:
Read the draft memo. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): {{0}} Requests written in the binder were sometimes missed because managers did not check it every day.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): Each of the requests {{1}} reviewed by a manager within one business day, and you will get a notice as soon as your swap is approved.
items.hint: For (A), what do all the details in paragraph 2 describe? For (B), cover up “of the requests” and read the sentence again.
items.explain:
Blank (A). The rest of paragraph 2 lists missed requests, torn or stained pages, an unrecorded swap, and open shifts that off-site employees could not see. All are problems with the binder, so the topic sentence is “The paper binder has caused several problems.”

Blank (B). The subject is “Each,” not “requests.” The phrase “of the requests” sits between the subject and the verb and can fool your ear. Each is singular, so the verb is “is.” “Are” is the tempting wrong answer because “requests” is right next to the blank.

options: The paper binder has caused several problems.
The break room is open to all employees from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.
Many employees prefer to work weekend shifts.
Please clock in at least five minutes before your shift.
why: This is about the break room's hours, but paragraph 2 lists problems with the binder. A topic sentence must cover the details that follow.
Paragraph 2 never discusses which shifts people prefer. This sentence does not cover missed requests, torn pages, or unrecorded swaps.
This is an unrelated instruction. It does not state what paragraph 2 is about.

options: is
are
were
being
why: You matched the verb to “requests,” which is the closest noun. The subject is “Each,” which is singular; “of the requests” only describes it.
“Were” is plural and past tense. The subject “Each” is singular, and the memo describes how the new system works now.
“Being” cannot serve as the main verb. “Each of the requests being reviewed…” would not be a complete clause.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, the author claims that sleep “is one of the times when learning actually happens.” Which detail from the passage best supports this claim?
items.hint: The best support shows that sleep leads to more learning, not just that the brain is busy.
items.explain:
Step 1. Restate the claim: sleep helps people learn.

Step 2. The best support must show that sleep leads to more learning. The word-pair study does: the sleepers remembered about 20 percent more.

Step 3. The 90-minute cycle is the most tempting choice because it shows the brain stays busy, but busy does not prove learning. The Luis and “switching off” details are views the author disagrees with.
options: People who slept after learning word pairs remembered about 20 percent more pairs than people who stayed awake.
The brain completes one cycle of sleep stages about every 90 minutes.
Luis has decided that every hour of sleep he skips is another hour of studying.
For much of history, people assumed that sleep was simply the brain switching off.
why: This shows the brain is active during sleep, but being active is not the same as learning. It does not show that people remember more.
This is the mistaken belief the author argues against, so it cannot support the author's claim.
This is the old idea the author says “began to fall apart.” It works against the claim, not for it.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author states that different stages of sleep “may help with different kinds of learning.” Which two details support this statement? Select two answers.
items.hint: A supporting detail here must name a stage of sleep and a kind of learning.
items.explain:
Step 1. The claim has two parts: different stages and different kinds of learning. A supporting detail must link a stage to a kind of learning.

Step 2. Deep sleep is linked to facts. REM sleep is linked to connecting ideas and practicing skills. Those are the two details.

Step 3. The 20 percent study is tempting because it is strong evidence, but it supports the general idea that sleep helps memory, not the idea that stages differ.
options: Deep sleep appears especially important for facts, such as dates, definitions, and formulas.
REM sleep seems to help the brain connect ideas and practice skills.
The brain completes one cycle of sleep stages about every 90 minutes.
People who slept after learning remembered about 20 percent more word pairs.
A new memory is first held in the hippocampus.
Luis is studying flash cards at 2 a.m.
why: This tells how often the stages repeat, not which kind of learning each stage helps.
This shows that sleep in general helps memory. It does not separate one stage from another or name different kinds of learning.
This tells where a memory starts. It says nothing about how different stages help different kinds of learning.
This is the opening example (a hook). It does not describe any stage of sleep.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 4, how many word pairs did the volunteers learn in the study? Type the number.
items.hint: Find the sentence in paragraph 4 that describes the list the volunteers learned.
items.explain:
Step 1. Go to paragraph 4, which describes the study.

Step 2. The second sentence says volunteers “learned a list of forty word pairs.”

Answer: 40. The paragraph also contains 8 (hours) and 20 (percent), which are easy to grab if you skim for any number.

mistakes.why: 20 is the percent of extra word pairs the sleepers remembered, not the number of pairs on the list. Reread the second sentence of paragraph 4.
Eight is the number of hours each group slept or stayed awake. The list length is in the sentence that describes what the volunteers learned.

items.prompt: Which sentence should be removed from paragraph 2 of the memo because it does not support the main idea of the paragraph?
items.hint: Paragraph 2 lists problems with the paper binder. Which sentence is not a problem with the binder?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the paragraph's main idea: the paper binder has caused several problems.

Step 2. Test each sentence. Missed requests, torn and stained pages, an unrecorded swap, and open shifts no one could see from outside the store are all binder problems.

Step 3. The new refrigerator is about the break room, not the binder. It is tempting to keep it because the binder is kept in the break room, but it does not describe a problem with the binder.
options: Requests written in the binder were sometimes missed because managers did not check it every day.
Last month, two employees showed up for the same shift because a swap was never recorded.
The break room will get a new refrigerator in May.
Finally, employees who were not at the store could not see which shifts were open.
why: Missed requests are a problem with the binder, so this sentence supports the paragraph and should stay.
An unrecorded swap is a problem caused by the binder. It is strong support and belongs.
Not being able to see open shifts from home is another binder problem. “Finally” marks it as the last item in the list.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category based on the passage.
items.hint: The central idea covers the whole passage. A supporting detail is a specific fact the passage gives. If you cannot point to it, it is not in the passage.
items.explain:
Central idea: “Sleep plays an active role in helping the brain store what a person learns.” This covers every paragraph and restates paragraph 1 (“one of the times when learning actually happens”).

Supporting details: The 90-minute cycle (paragraph 2) supports the idea that the sleeping brain is busy. The word-pair study (paragraph 4) supports the idea that sleep improves memory.

Not in the passage: The passage never states how many hours a person needs to pass a test, and it never mentions coffee. These may sound reasonable, but neither can be found in the text.
choices: Sleep plays an active role in helping the brain store what a person learns.
The brain completes one cycle of sleep stages about every 90 minutes.
In one study, people who slept after learning word pairs remembered about 20 percent more pairs than people who stayed awake.
Adults need at least ten hours of sleep the night before a test in order to pass it.
Drinking coffee while studying late at night improves memory.
items.why: The most common mistake is placing the ten-hours statement under “Supporting detail” because it sounds like sleep advice. The passage never gives a number of hours needed to pass a test. Coffee is never mentioned either.

items.prompt:
Denise wants to add a sentence at the beginning of paragraph 4 of the memo that states the paragraph's main idea. Which sentence works best?

{{0}} Training will be held in the break room on March 24 and March 26 at 2:00 p.m.
items.hint: List the three things paragraph 4 offers. What do they have in common?
items.explain:
Step 1. List the details in paragraph 4: training times, a printed guide by the time clock, and help from the assistant manager.

Step 2. What do they share? Each one is a way to get help learning the app.

Step 3. So the topic sentence is “Help is available for anyone who is new to the app.” The Jamal sentence is tempting because he is named in the paragraph, but it covers only one detail and adds a fact the memo never gives.

options: Help is available for anyone who is new to the app.
The paper binder will be removed from the break room on April 1.
Jamal Pierce has worked at the store for six years.
Some employees may prefer to keep using the binder.
why: This is about removing the binder, but paragraph 4 describes training, a printed guide, and help from Jamal. It does not cover those details.
This is not stated in the memo, and it is too narrow: Jamal is only one of three kinds of help the paragraph offers.
This is not stated, and it works against the paragraph, which is about helping people use the app.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the memo.

The main purpose of the memo is to {{0}}. The detail that best supports the claim that the app “fixes these problems” is that {{1}}.
items.hint: For the first blank, reread paragraph 1. For the second, match a problem from paragraph 2 to a solution in paragraph 3.
items.explain:
Blank 1. Paragraph 1 says the memo “explains why we are making the change and how the new system will work.” Paragraphs 2 and 3 do exactly that, and paragraph 4 explains how to get help. So the purpose is to explain the switch and how it works.

Blank 2. The binder's problems were missed and unrecorded requests. A detail that proves the app fixes them must show requests being handled: each request is reviewed within one business day, and employees are notified when a swap is approved. Training and the guide are tempting because they are about the app, but they do not fix anything.

options: explain the switch to the scheduling app and how it will work
announce training times for the new app
warn the two employees who showed up for the same shift
announce that the break room is getting a new refrigerator
why: This is too narrow. Training is one detail in paragraph 4; most of the memo explains why the store is switching and how the app works.
This is distorted. The double-booked shift is one example of a binder problem; the memo does not warn anyone.
This is the irrelevant sentence in paragraph 2, not the purpose of the memo.

options: each request is reviewed within one business day, and employees are notified when a swap is approved
training will be held on March 24 and March 26
a printed guide will be posted next to the time clock
the change begins on April 1
why: Training helps people learn the app, but it does not show that the app solves any of the binder's problems.
The guide is a way to learn the app. It does not show the app fixing missed or unrecorded swaps.
This tells when the change starts. It does not show that any problem is fixed.

items.skill: How a paragraph develops the central idea
items.prompt: How does paragraph 4 contribute to the development of the central idea of the passage?
items.hint: Paragraph 4 begins, “Experiments support this idea.” What idea, and what kind of support?
items.explain:
Step 1. Read the first sentence of paragraph 4: “Experiments support this idea.” “This idea” refers back to paragraph 3: sleep strengthens new memories.

Step 2. The rest of paragraph 4 describes a study in which the people who slept remembered about 20 percent more word pairs, and notes that similar studies found similar results. That is experimental evidence.

Step 3. The opposing-view choice is a trap for readers who notice that the paragraph compares two groups; the comparison actually supports the author.
options: It provides experimental evidence that sleeping after learning improves memory.
It describes the different stages the brain moves through during a night of sleep.
It presents an opposing view that sleep has little effect on memory.
It gives practical advice for planning study time before a test.
why: This describes paragraphs 2 and 5, which explain the stages of sleep. Paragraph 4 describes a study.
This reverses the paragraph. Paragraph 4 supports the link between sleep and memory; the sleepers remembered more.
This describes paragraph 6, which begins “For learners, the message is practical.”

items.prompt: A student is writing a summary of the passage. Which detail is least important to include in the summary?
items.hint: Which detail could you remove without losing any of the author's key points?
items.explain:
Step 1. A summary keeps the central idea and key points and leaves out minor details and examples.

Step 2. The memory-storage statement is the key point of paragraph 3. The “people who sleep remember more” statement is the conclusion of paragraph 4. The “study, then sleep” statement is the main advice of paragraph 6.

Step 3. Luis at his kitchen table is a hook that draws readers in. The passage's point does not depend on Luis, so this detail is least important. It is easy to keep because it is vivid and comes first, but vivid is not the same as important.
options: Luis is studying flash cards at his kitchen table at 2 a.m.
During sleep, the brain strengthens new memories and moves them into longer-term storage.
People who sleep after learning tend to remember more than people who stay awake.
Studying and then getting a full night of sleep works better than studying all night.
why: This is the key point of paragraph 3. Leaving it out would remove the explanation of how sleep helps learning.
This is the conclusion of the research in paragraph 4. A summary needs it as the main evidence.
This is the main advice of paragraph 6 and restates the central idea. It belongs in a summary.

items.prompt: The author does not state the central idea in one sentence. Which statement best expresses the implied central idea of the passage?
items.hint: Write one short note for each paragraph. Then ask: what caused the disaster, and how did it end?
items.explain:
Step 1. List each paragraph's point: farmers plowed up the grass that held the soil (paragraph 1); drought and wind blew the bare soil away (paragraph 2); families suffered and many left (paragraph 3); conservation methods helped the soil stay put (paragraph 4).

Step 2. Put them together: removing the grass plus drought caused the Dust Bowl, and new methods helped the land recover.

Step 3. The tractor choice is tempting because it links two real details, but it invents a cause-and-effect the passage never states.
options: Plowing up the prairie, then a long drought, created the Dust Bowl; new farming methods later helped hold the soil.
A massive dust storm known as Black Sunday swept across the plains on April 14, 1935.
Droughts and the dust storms they cause have brought disaster to farmers throughout human history.
The new gasoline tractors that farmers used to plow up the prairie caused the long drought that created the Dust Bowl.
why: This is too narrow. Black Sunday is one detail from paragraph 2; it leaves out the cause, the effects on families, and the recovery.
This is too broad. The passage is about one disaster in one region in the 1930s, not droughts and dust storms throughout history.
This is distorted. Tractors were used to plow up the grass; the passage never says they caused the drought. The drought was a separate event that began in the early 1930s.

items.prompt: Which choice is the best summary of the passage?
items.hint: Check each choice for three things: does it cover the whole passage, is every fact accurate, and is it free of opinion?
items.explain:
Step 1. A summary must cover each part: cause (plowed grass), event (drought and dust storms), effects (illness, people leaving), and response (conservation, returning rain).

Step 2. The “After farmers plowed up the prairie grass” choice covers all four accurately, in the writer's own words, with no opinion.

Step 3. The shelterbelt choice is tempting because shelterbelts are in the passage, but it changes what they did and when.
options: After farmers plowed up the prairie grass, a 1930s drought let winds blow the dry soil away in huge storms that sickened people and drove many from the plains. New farming methods, tree rows, and returning rain helped hold the soil.
On April 14, 1935, a storm called Black Sunday turned day into night, and families hung wet sheets over their windows, but the dust still coated their food and furniture.
The Dust Bowl was the worst disaster in American history, and farmers today should never use tractors.

Shelterbelts of trees planted by the government ended the drought on the plains by 1935, so the dust storms stopped and most of the families who had left for California were able to return to their farms the next year.
why: This is too narrow. It gives vivid details from paragraphs 2 and 3 but leaves out the cause and the recovery.
This adds opinions and claims the author never makes. A summary must be objective and stay within the passage.
This is distorted. Trees slowed the wind; they did not end the drought. Rain returned around 1940, and the passage never says families returned.

stimuli.title: Fixing Instead of Tossing: The Rise of Repair Cafés
stimuli.html:
[1] On the second Saturday of every month, the fellowship hall of a church in Millbrook fills with broken things: lamps that will not light, toasters that will not toast, jeans with split seams, a vacuum cleaner that only hums. Their owners have come to the Millbrook Repair Café, where volunteers fix items for free while the owners watch and learn. Gatherings like this one, which began in the Netherlands in 2009, have spread to thousands of communities around the world. They are popular because they help people save money, keep useful things out of landfills, and pass along skills that many people never learned.

[2] The savings are easy to see. A new vacuum cleaner can cost more than $150, while a replacement belt costs a few dollars. Last year, Millbrook volunteers worked on 412 items and got 287 of them working again. Most owners said that without the café, they would have thrown the item away and bought a new one.

[3] Each repair also keeps waste out of the landfill. Small appliances and electronics contain metals and plastics that do not break down. When a toaster is fixed, it is not buried, and a new one does not have to be manufactured, packaged, and shipped.

[4] Perhaps the most lasting benefit, however, is what people learn. Volunteers do not carry a broken item into a back room. They sit beside its owner and explain each step: how to open the case safely, how to test a cord, how to find the part that failed. Several regular visitors have become volunteers themselves. “I used to think only experts could fix things,” said Tanya Brooks, who now repairs bicycles at the café. “Now I'm the one teaching.”

[5] Repair cafés do face limits. Many newer products are glued shut or built so that parts cannot be replaced, and some items are simply too damaged to save. Still, organizers say each fixed lamp or mended coat shows that “broken” does not have to mean “finished.”

stimuli.title: The Last Bus from Harbor Industrial Park
stimuli.html: Until last year, the last evening bus from Harbor Industrial Park left at 5:15 p.m., but most factory shifts there end at 6:00. Workers without cars paid for rides home or walked more than two miles along a highway with no sidewalk. In January, the transit agency moved the last bus to 6:20 p.m. Since then, ridership on that route has tripled, and two factories report that fewer new workers quit in their first month.

stimuli.title: Gardens on Empty Lots
stimuli.html:
[1] Ten years ago, the city of Dunmore had more than 900 vacant lots, many of them filled with weeds, broken glass, and dumped tires. Today, about 60 of those lots are community gardens, where neighbors grow tomatoes, collards, peppers, and flowers. The gardens began as a small experiment by one neighborhood group. They have grown into one of the city's most successful programs, providing fresh food, safer blocks, and places where neighbors get to know one another.

[2] Food is the most obvious harvest. Many of the gardens are in neighborhoods where the nearest full grocery store is more than a mile away. Gardeners grow far more than they can eat, and most gardens donate the extra to food pantries. Last summer, Dunmore's gardens gave away more than 18,000 pounds of produce.

[3] The gardens have also changed how blocks feel. A lot that once attracted illegal dumping now has people working in it every evening. A local university compared blocks that had a garden with similar blocks that did not. Over three years, the garden blocks had fewer calls to police about vandalism and dumping.

[4] Just as important, the gardens bring people together. Neighbors who had lived on the same street for years without speaking now share tools, swap seeds, and trade recipes. Older gardeners teach children how to plant and when to harvest. “I came for the tomatoes,” said longtime gardener Ruth Okafor. “I stayed for the people.”

[5] Keeping the gardens going is not easy, however. Most depend on volunteers, and a garden can fall apart when its leaders move away. Some lots are still owned by the city, which could sell them to developers. Garden leaders are now asking the city to protect the most successful gardens permanently.

stimuli.title: Reminders at the County Clinic
stimuli.html: For years, the county clinic mailed appointment reminders a week ahead, and about one patient in four still missed a visit. Last spring, the clinic began sending text messages two days before each appointment, with a link to reschedule. By fall, missed appointments had dropped to about one in ten, and the clinic was able to see forty more patients each month in time slots that used to sit empty.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.explain: The last sentence of paragraph 1 states the central idea: repair cafés are popular “because they help people save money, keep useful things out of landfills, and pass along skills.” Paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 each develop one of those three benefits, and paragraph 5 notes limits. The “save money, reduce waste, and learn repair skills” choice covers all of it. The 287-items choice is tempting because it is a precise fact, but it describes only one paragraph.
options: Repair cafés, where volunteers fix items for free, help people save money, reduce waste, and learn repair skills.
Millbrook volunteers got 287 broken items working again last year.
Repair cafés can fix nearly any broken product, including newer items that are glued shut or built without replaceable parts.
Companies should be required by law to make products that are easier to repair.
why: This is too narrow. It is one number from paragraph 2 and leaves out waste, skills, and limits.
This is distorted. Paragraph 5 says many glued-shut products and products whose parts cannot be replaced are hard to repair, and some items are too damaged to save.
This is not stated. The passage never calls for a law. It is an opinion a reader might add.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 4 that best states the main idea of that paragraph.
items.explain: Paragraph 4 opens with its main idea: “Perhaps the most lasting benefit, however, is what people learn.” Every sentence after it is evidence of learning: volunteers explain each step, visitors become volunteers, and Tanya Brooks now teaches others. Do not skip a sentence just because it contains “however”; here the transition word sits inside the main idea itself.
spans: Perhaps the most lasting benefit, however, is what people learn.
Volunteers do not carry a broken item into a back room.
They sit beside its owner and explain each step: how to open the case safely, how to test a cord, how to find the part that failed.
Several regular visitors have become volunteers themselves.
“I used to think only experts could fix things,” said Tanya Brooks, who now repairs bicycles at the café.
“Now I'm the one teaching.”
items.why: A common wrong click is the sentence about volunteers explaining each step, because it is long and specific. It is one example of what people learn. Another trap is the Tanya Brooks quotation, which is a single person's story.

items.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that repair cafés help people save money?
items.explain: To support “save money,” a detail must compare costs. The vacuum example does: more than $150 for a new machine versus a few dollars for a belt. Each other detail is true but supports a different point: waste (paragraph 3), skills (paragraph 4), or history (paragraph 1).
options: A new vacuum cleaner can cost more than $150, while a replacement belt costs a few dollars.
Small appliances and electronics contain metals and plastics that do not break down.
Several regular visitors have become volunteers themselves.
Repair cafés began in the Netherlands in 2009.
why: This supports the idea that repairs reduce waste (paragraph 3), not that they save money.
This supports the idea that people learn skills (paragraph 4). It says nothing about money.
This is background history. It does not show anyone saving money.

items.prompt: Which two details support the idea that repair cafés pass along repair skills? Select two answers.
items.explain: Skills are passed along when someone learns to do the work. Volunteers explaining each step shows teaching, and visitors who become volunteers shows that the learning worked. The 412-items detail is tempting because it shows a lot of activity, but activity is not the same as teaching.
options: Volunteers sit beside each owner and explain every step of the repair.
Several regular visitors have become volunteers themselves.
Millbrook volunteers worked on 412 items last year.
Many newer products are glued shut.
Most owners would otherwise have thrown the item away and bought a new one.
Repair cafés have spread to thousands of communities.
why: This counts repairs. It does not show anyone learning how to do them.
This is a limit on what can be fixed, not evidence that people learn skills.
This supports saving money and reducing waste, not learning skills.
This shows the idea is popular, not that skills are being taught.

items.prompt: Which choice is the best summary of the passage?
items.explain: A good summary states the central idea and the key point of each part: what a repair café is, the three benefits (paragraphs 2–4), and the limits (paragraph 5). The “volunteers fix items for free as owners watch and learn” choice does this accurately, without opinion. The Tanya Brooks choice is tempting because it is memorable, but a single example is not a summary.
options: At repair cafés, volunteers fix items for free as owners watch and learn. The cafés save money, reduce landfill waste, and teach skills, though some products are too damaged or too hard to open.
Tanya Brooks used to think only experts could fix things, but now she repairs bicycles at the Millbrook Repair Café.
Repair cafés are the best way to fight waste, and every town should start one as soon as possible.

Repair cafés charge a small fee to fix broken lamps, toasters, and vacuums in a back room, and because their volunteers are experts, they can repair almost anything people bring in, even products that are glued shut.
why: This is too narrow. It tells one person's story from paragraph 4 and leaves out money, waste, and limits.
This adds opinions (“the best way,” “every town should”) that the author never states. A summary must be objective.
This is distorted. Repairs are free, owners sit beside the volunteers rather than waiting while items go to a back room, and paragraph 5 says glued-shut and badly damaged items often cannot be saved.

items.prompt: Which paragraph develops the idea that repair cafés keep useful things out of landfills? Type the paragraph number.
items.explain: Paragraph 1 lists three benefits. Each of the next three paragraphs develops one: paragraph 2 (money), paragraph 3 (waste: “Each repair also keeps waste out of the landfill”), paragraph 4 (skills). Answer: 3.

mistakes.why: Paragraph 2 develops the money benefit (the vacuum belt and the items owners would have replaced). Look for the paragraph about things not breaking down and not being buried.
Paragraph 1 names all three benefits in its last sentence, but it does not develop any of them. The paragraph that explains the landfill benefit comes later.
Paragraph 5 describes the limits of repair cafés, not the landfill benefit.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the implied main idea of the paragraph?
items.explain: List the details: the bus left before shifts ended; workers paid for rides or walked along a dangerous highway; the bus was moved to 6:20; ridership tripled and fewer new workers quit. Together they show that matching the bus to shift times made it much more useful to workers. The tripled-ridership choice is tempting because it is the most striking result, but it is only one detail.
options: Moving the last bus to fit factory shift times has made the route far more useful to workers.
Ridership on the route has tripled since January.
Every factory should run its own shuttle bus for workers.
The transit agency built a sidewalk along the highway so that workers could walk home safely after their shifts.
why: This is too narrow. It is one result and leaves out the problem (the bus left before shifts ended) and the change that fixed it.
This is not stated. The paragraph never suggests factories should run buses; it describes what the transit agency did.
This is distorted. The paragraph says workers walked along a highway with no sidewalk; nothing says one was built.

items.prompt:
Complete each statement about the paragraph.

“The Harbor Industrial Park bus route” is {{0}}.

“Two factories report that fewer new workers quit in their first month” is {{1}}.

As an answer to “What is the main idea of the paragraph?”, the statement “The transit agency added three buses to the route” is {{2}}.
items.explain:
Blank 1: a phrase that names the subject and cannot be true or false is a topic.

Blank 2: a specific fact that shows the change worked is a supporting detail.

Blank 3: the paragraph says the agency moved the last bus to a later time and that ridership tripled; it never says any buses were added. The statement takes the real change and twists it, so it is distorted.

options: a topic
a main idea
a supporting detail
why: A main idea must be a complete sentence that can be true or false. This is a phrase that only names the subject.
A supporting detail is a specific fact that proves the main idea. This phrase states no fact; it only names what the paragraph is about.

options: a topic
a main idea
a supporting detail
why: A topic is a word or phrase. This is a full sentence that reports a specific result.
This is one specific result, not the overall point. The main idea must cover the whole paragraph, including the problem and the schedule change.

options: too narrow
too broad
distorted
why: Too narrow means a true detail that covers only part of the text. This statement is not true: the agency moved the last bus to a later time; it did not add buses.
Too broad means bigger than the text. This statement is about this one route, so it is not too broad; it is inaccurate.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.explain: The end of paragraph 1 states the main claim: the gardens provide “fresh food, safer blocks, and places where neighbors get to know one another.” Paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 develop those three benefits, and paragraph 5 explains the challenges. Only the “fresh food, safer blocks, and closer neighbors” choice covers all five paragraphs. The 18,000-pounds choice is tempting because it is impressive, but it describes only paragraph 2.
options: Dunmore's community gardens have provided fresh food, safer blocks, and closer neighbors, though they need steady support.
Dunmore's gardens gave away more than 18,000 pounds of produce last summer.
Community gardens have replaced all of Dunmore's more than 900 vacant lots, ending the problem of weeds, glass, and dumped tires.
The city of Dunmore should give every vacant lot to a neighborhood group.
why: This is too narrow. It is one number from paragraph 2 and leaves out safety, community, and the challenges.
This is distorted. About 60 of more than 900 vacant lots became gardens, not all of them, so the problem has not ended.
This is not stated. The passage reports that leaders want the most successful gardens protected; it never says every lot should be given away.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 4 that best states the main idea of that paragraph.
items.explain: Paragraph 4 opens with its main idea: “Just as important, the gardens bring people together.” The rest of the paragraph gives evidence: neighbors who never spoke now share, older gardeners teach children, and a longtime gardener says she stayed for the people. “Just as important” is a transition, but here it sits inside the main idea sentence.
spans: Just as important, the gardens bring people together.
Neighbors who had lived on the same street for years without speaking now share tools, swap seeds, and trade recipes.
Older gardeners teach children how to plant and when to harvest.
“I came for the tomatoes,” said longtime gardener Ruth Okafor.
“I stayed for the people.”
items.why: A common wrong click is the sentence about neighbors sharing tools and trading recipes, because it is detailed. It is one example of people coming together. The Ruth Okafor quotation is also only one person's view.

items.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that the gardens have made blocks safer?
items.explain: To support “safer blocks,” a detail must show less crime or danger. The university comparison does: garden blocks had fewer police calls about vandalism and dumping. Each other choice is true but supports a different point.
options: Garden blocks had fewer police calls about vandalism and dumping than similar blocks without gardens.
Last summer, Dunmore's gardens gave away more than 18,000 pounds of produce to local food pantries.
Older gardeners teach children how to plant and when to harvest.
Some garden lots are still owned by the city, which could sell them to developers who want to build on them.
why: This supports the food benefit (paragraph 2), not safety.
This supports the idea that gardens bring people together (paragraph 4), not that blocks are safer.
This is a challenge the gardens face (paragraph 5). It does not show any change in safety.

items.prompt: Which two details support the idea that the gardens provide fresh food? Select two answers.
items.explain: Paragraph 2 develops the food benefit. Two details show the gardens actually producing food for people: gardeners grow extra and donate it, and the gardens gave away more than 18,000 pounds of produce. The recipe-trading detail is tempting because it mentions food, but it shows neighbors connecting, not gardens providing food.
options: Gardeners grow more than they can eat, and most gardens donate the extra to food pantries.
Last summer, the gardens gave away more than 18,000 pounds of produce.
Neighbors share tools, swap seeds, and trade recipes.
Dunmore once had more than 900 vacant lots.
A lot that once attracted dumping now has people working in it every evening.
Some lots are still owned by the city.
why: This shows neighbors connecting (paragraph 4). Trading recipes is about cooking, not about the gardens producing food.
This describes the problem before the gardens existed. It says nothing about food.
This supports the idea that blocks feel safer (paragraph 3), not the food benefit.
This is a challenge from paragraph 5, not evidence of fresh food.

items.prompt: Which choice is the best summary of the passage?
items.explain: A good summary gives the central idea and each key point: what changed (lots became gardens), the three benefits, and the challenges. The “About 60 of Dunmore's vacant lots” choice does all of this accurately and without opinion. The distorted choice is tempting because it mentions food and police calls, but it exaggerates both.
options: About 60 of Dunmore's vacant lots are now gardens that supply food, make blocks safer, and bring neighbors together. Because they rely on volunteers and some sit on city land, leaders want the best ones protected.
Ruth Okafor came to her garden for the tomatoes but stayed for the people.

Community gardens are the most important thing a city can build, and every city should turn all of its empty lots into gardens right away, even if that means turning down developers who want to buy the land.
Dunmore's gardens now grow so much food that the city no longer needs full grocery stores, and police calls about vandalism and dumping have stopped completely on every block with a garden.
why: This is too narrow. It is one quotation from paragraph 4 and leaves out food, safety, and the challenges.
This adds the reader's opinion (“most important,” “every city should”). A summary must be objective.
This is distorted. The passage says the gardens donate extra food and that garden blocks had fewer police calls, not that stores are unneeded or that calls stopped.

items.prompt: Which paragraph develops the idea that the gardens have made blocks safer? Type the paragraph number.
items.explain: Paragraph 1 lists three benefits. Paragraph 2 develops food, paragraph 3 develops safety (“The gardens have also changed how blocks feel,” followed by the police-call study), and paragraph 4 develops community. Answer: 3.

mistakes.why: Paragraph 4 develops the idea that gardens bring people together. Look for the paragraph about dumping, vandalism, and police calls.
Paragraph 1 names the three benefits, including safer blocks, but it does not develop them. The evidence comes later.
Paragraph 2 develops the food benefit, not safety.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the implied main idea of the paragraph?
items.explain: List the details: mailed reminders left about one in four patients missing visits; the clinic switched to texts with a reschedule link; missed visits fell to about one in ten; the clinic saw forty more patients a month. Together they show the switch reduced missed appointments and let the clinic serve more people. The “almost no patients” choice is tempting because it sounds like a success story, but it overstates the result.
options: Switching to text reminders helped the clinic cut missed appointments and see more patients.
The clinic sends text messages two days before each appointment.
Mailed reminders should no longer be used by any doctor's office.
Since the clinic began sending texts, almost no patients miss appointments.
why: This is too narrow. It describes the new method but not its results, the fewer missed visits and the forty extra patients.
This is not stated. The paragraph describes one clinic's results; it never says what every office should do.
This is distorted. About one patient in ten still misses a visit. Missed appointments dropped; they did not nearly disappear.

Complete each statement about the paragraph.

“Appointment reminders at the county clinic” is {{0}}.

“By fall, missed appointments had dropped to about one in ten” is {{1}}.

As an answer to “What is the main idea of the paragraph?”, the statement “The clinic stopped mailing reminders because postage became too expensive” is {{2}}.

Blank 1: a phrase that names the subject is a topic.

Blank 2: a specific result that shows the change worked is a supporting detail.

Blank 3: the paragraph never says why the clinic switched, and it never mentions postage. A reason invented by the reader is not stated.

a main idea

A supporting detail is a specific fact. This phrase states no fact; it only names what the paragraph is about.

a main idea

why: A topic is a word or phrase. This is a full sentence that reports a specific result.
This is one result, not the overall point. The main idea must also cover the switch to texts and the extra patients seen.

vocab.def: The subject of a text, usually named in a word or short phrase.
The most important point an author makes about the topic of a paragraph, stated as a complete sentence.
vocab.example: Public libraries now play a major role in helping people find work.

vocab.def: The main idea of a whole passage. The GED often uses this term.
vocab.example: Cities are starting to treat trees as necessary public equipment.

vocab.def: The sentence in a paragraph that states its main idea, often but not always the first sentence.
vocab.example: “Employers benefit as well.” opens a paragraph about how apprenticeships help companies.

vocab.def: A fact, example, number, reason, description, or quotation that explains or proves the main idea.
vocab.example: Homes shaded by trees used about 12 percent less electricity for cooling.

vocab.def: A main idea that the author writes directly in one sentence of the text.
vocab.example: “A credit score can affect much more than whether you get a loan.”

vocab.def: A main idea the author does not state directly; the reader figures it out from the details.
vocab.example: Details about closed grocery stores and long bus trips imply that healthy food has become hard to get.

vocab.def: A short restatement of a text's central idea and key points in your own words, without opinions or minor details.
vocab.example: A three-sentence summary of a one-page article.

vocab.def: Restating one idea or sentence in your own words, at about the same length as the original.
vocab.example: “Trees catch rain” paraphrases “leaves and branches catch rainwater and slow its fall.”

vocab.def: Nonfiction writing that explains or gives facts, such as articles, reports, letters, and workplace documents.
vocab.example: A news article about city tree planting.

vocab.def: Closely connected to the main idea. A detail that is not relevant does not belong in the paragraph.
vocab.example: In a paragraph about a room's advantages, a sentence about repainting a different building is not relevant.

vocab.def: Based on the facts in the text, not on personal feelings or opinions. Summaries should be objective.
vocab.example: Objective: “The author explains that …” Not objective: “The author makes a great point.”

vocab.def: A word or phrase that connects ideas and signals a shift, such as however, also, or as a result.
vocab.example: “Cooling is only part of the story, however.”

vocab.def: An opening sentence, story, question, or common belief that grabs the reader's attention. It is often not the main idea.
vocab.example: “Almost every home has a drawer full of old phone chargers.” opens a paragraph about recycling electronics.

vocab.def: A wrong answer choice built to sound right. The four common traps are too narrow, too broad, not stated, and distorted.
vocab.example: “Corbin has a new coffee shop” is a too-narrow trap for a question about Corbin's revival.

notes:
Week 1 RLA Study Sheet: Main Idea, Details, Summarizing

Key terms

  • Topic: subject in a word or phrase
  • Main idea: author's point about the topic, as a sentence (can be true or false)
  • Central idea: main idea of a whole passage
  • Supporting detail: fact, example, number, reason, or quote that proves the main idea
  • Summary: central idea plus key points, in your own words, short and objective

Where main ideas live

  1. First sentence (most common)
  2. After a hook or turn (however, but, in fact)
  3. Last sentence
  4. Implied (you write it)

For a passage: title, end of paragraph 1, conclusion.

Finding an implied main idea

  1. List the details.
  2. What do they have in common?
  3. What does the author want me to understand?
  4. Write one sentence.
  5. Umbrella test.

Writing a summary

  1. Central idea in one sentence
  2. Two to four key points
  3. Drop small examples, numbers, quotes
  4. No opinions, no outside facts
  5. Check accuracy against the text

Umbrella test: The main idea must cover every important detail. Too small = too narrow. Too big = too broad.

Answer traps

TrapSignAsk yourself
Too narrowTrue, but only one detail or paragraphDoes it cover the whole text?
Too broadAbout the whole world or a bigger subjectDoes the text really discuss all of this?
Not statedOpinion or outside knowledgeCan I point to where it says this?
DistortedA detail changed, reversed, or exaggeratedDoes it match the text exactly in meaning?

“Best supports” questions

  1. Restate the claim in your own words.
  2. Ask of each choice: if this is true, does it prove this claim?
  3. Cut details that prove a different point or are only background.

Strategy: Predict, match, test. Say the answer in your own words before reading the choices. Then match it to a choice, test it with the umbrella, and name the trap on every choice you cut.

Common mistakes: picking the first sentence automatically; picking a true detail; using background knowledge; adding opinions to a summary.
